approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and lower Ptarmigan Ridge, then 1,000 ft down to the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Wonderland Trail from Mowich Lake about 4 miles to Spray Park, then the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge. At about 8,300 ft the route DESCENDS roughly 1,000 ft onto the North Mowich Glacier and crosses to the base of the face.

There are two lines from about 12,500 ft. The original variation cuts left into an hourglass of snow, ice and rock, gaining a ledge that leads to a 40-50 degree ramp to the top. The harder variation cuts right through a couple of AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow to the same high point.

Mowich Lake has had no public road access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025; reaching it now means a long walk in from another park entrance.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug
hazards: Ice steps and steep snow with rockfall exposure
A 1,000 ft descent onto the glacier on the approach, which must be reclimbed if you retreat
Remote approach with limited bailout options
Crevasses on the North Mowich crossing
No road access on this side of the park since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first thing to get right is that you lose a thousand feet on the way in. At about 8,300 ft on lower Ptarmigan Ridge you stop climbing and drop onto the North Mowich Glacier. A party that keeps gaining height is on Ptarmigan Ridge, not on this face, and will not find out for hours.

Four climbs come off this wall and they are separated by where the steep ground is, not by the walk in.

The positive test for this route is an absence, which is unusual but it is the reliable one here: there is no constriction low down. You cross the schrund and climb open face. The hourglass on this route is high — around 12,500 ft — not at the bottom. So if your first 50 ft above the schrund is a steep pinch of mixed rock and ice, you are on the North Mowich Headwall and you crossed too far round.

The rock band settles it definitively, and it is the one place the two lines behave oppositely. On this face, at the rock band you can traverse right several hundred feet and skirt the band entirely. On the North Mowich Headwall you cannot: you have to clear the band, at 5th class in a lean year. If the band in front of you has to be climbed rather than walked around, you are one line over.

Schrund check: the bergschrund under the central face has been passed by a bypass through a rock band on climber's left. If the only way across in front of you is beside a pair of twin gendarmes, that is the Edmunds Headwall's schrund and you are further round the mountain than you meant to be.

Choose your variation before 12,500 ft, not at it. Left is the original: an hourglass, a ledge, a 40-50 degree ramp. Right is harder: AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow. They rejoin, but you cannot swap once you are on one.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the bivy between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Mowich Face approach and is shared with three other climbs: Mowich Lake, the Wonderland Trail through Spray Park, then cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock onto the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge.

The bivouac for this route sits at roughly 9,600 to 10,000 ft on the divide between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers. Two days to reach it is the normal plan rather than a cautious one.

From the bivy the climbing starts almost at once. Above the hourglass, roughly 2,000 ft of about 45-degree snow leads to a rock band; the documented way through is to look for an arch in the rock on the right, traverse left, then work back right to gain the ice cap. In a low-snow year that band can demand unprotected loose 5th-class climbing, which is the part of this route that changes most from season to season.

Mowich Lake has had no public road access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025; reaching it now means a long walk in from another park entrance.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, climbed early in the day for rockfall
hazards: A rock band crux that can require unprotected loose 5th-class climbing in low-snow years
Sustained steep ice with rockfall exposure — climb it early
Crevasses and avalanche debris on the glacier crossing out of camp
Remote position, two-day approach, and no quick retreat from high on the face
No road access on this side of the park since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Four climbs share this wall and this camp. From the divide bivy the discriminator is which glacier you cross and where the hourglass is.

The positive test, and it is the strong one: this route's hourglass is low. Within 40 to 50 ft of leaving the bivy you should be in a steep constriction of mixed rock and ice. First ground, immediately, right off the deck. That is the North Mowich Headwall's signature.

The negative that matters most is the Central Mowich Face next door, and it also has an hourglass — but at 12,500 ft, not at 10,000. So the question at the base is not 'is there an hourglass on this route' but 'is the hourglass here, now, in the first 50 ft'. If your first 2,000 ft is open snow with no constriction at all, you are on the Central Mowich Face and your hourglass is still two thousand feet above you.

The other negative is the Edmunds Headwall, and it is settled by the schrund: the Edmunds is entered by bypassing its bergschrund on climber's left near a pair of twin gendarmes. If you crossed the schrund beside two rock towers, you are on the Edmunds and you crossed the wrong glacier out of camp.

Sequence check once committed, in order: 40-50 ft hourglass of rock and ice, then roughly 2,000 ft of sustained 45-degree snow, then a rock band that has to be cleared. If the rock band arrives early, you are not on this line. If it never arrives, you traversed off onto the Central Mowich, which skirts the band entirely by going right.

What being too far round looks like: if you left camp and CLIMBED rather than crossing a glacier, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake, Rampart Ridge, and the cairned Alta turnoff on the Lila Lake trail
approach_variants.notes:
From the Rachel Lake trailhead at 2,800 ft, at the end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Road from I-90 exit 62, take Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first 2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek at a gentle grade with reliable water throughout.

At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses the creek and hits the section known locally as the mile from hell: a heavily rooted, rocky climb gaining roughly 1,300 ft in a mile with big step-ups and no switchbacks. It is the fitness crux of the day, not a technical one.

At Rachel Lake, 4,700 ft, a use trail branches right near the outhouse, skirts the lake's north side, and switchbacks steeply about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest at about 5,100 ft. At the ridge junction go right toward Lila Lake; the left branch leads to Rampart Lakes and is not this route. After about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork: Lila Lake is straight ahead, and the climbers' path up Alta's south ridge is the left branch.
approach_variants.season: July to October. The route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge
hazards: Sustained exposure along the ridge crest, including a section skirting a cliff edge
Three false summits and a class 3 downclimb crux near the top
Loose rock and large step-ups on the initial climbers' path
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long exposed crest
Lingering snow in the approach gully in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The takeoff is a cairn on the Lila Lake Trail, not anything in the Rampart Lakes basin. At the ridge-top junction above Rachel Lake turn right (left goes to Rampart Lakes); about 0.3 mile along, a cairn marks a fork where Lila Lake is straight on and the unsigned climbers' path to Alta goes left. If you find yourself among the Rampart tarns, you took the wrong branch at the ridge.

Where it puts you: the climbers' path climbs Alta's south ridge, steep, loose and shadeless at first, before easing onto the narrow crest that leads to the summit block.

What the ridge then does, so you can count your way along it: three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, at least one near-vertical step of 6 to 8 ft with good holds and serious exposure, and a class 3 DOWNCLIMB crux near the top. A party that has crossed one bump and thinks it is at the summit is two bumps early.

And the one place where the finding is a warning rather than a direction: there is a section where the path skirts a cliff edge. Fall consequences there are serious. This route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge, and it is not a place for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.

A second, independent description of the same takeoff: an unsigned climbers' path marked by a cairn leaves the maintained trail near the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake junction and climbs the south ridge. Steep, loose, big steps and no shade at first, then it moderates onto the knife-edge crest.

approach_variants.name: High Pass and the Gargett Mine, then the long sidehill under Larrabee to the South AmBo Saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Contamination warning before anything else: this is AMERICAN Border Peak, 7,998 ft, in Washington. CANADIAN Border Peak is about a kilometre north across the international line and is a different mountain with its own routes, reached from British Columbia. Beta for the two is routinely mixed up because both are called 'Border Peak'. Everything here is the Washington approach from Twin Lakes.

From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft, take the High Pass Trail; at a quarter mile it splits from the short spur up Winchester Mountain — stay left, north. The trail contours the west side of Winchester, dips across Low Pass, and climbs to High Pass near 5,960 ft, about two miles and 750 ft of gain, where Mount Baker comes into view south.

At High Pass leave the maintained tread and follow the climbers' path north and west down to the old Gargett Mine workings around 5,400 ft. The mine creek is the last reliable water until lingering snow high on the peak.

From the mine, traverse north and contour onto Mount Larrabee's southwest and west flanks. This is a long, unmarked, exposed sidehill of well over a mile across steep talus, scree, heather and brush.

Most parties camp at Gargett Basin or in the moraine bowl and climb from there rather than pushing summit day from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and never on wet grass or wet rock
hazards: Chronic rockfall — the defining hazard of this approach, helmets on from the Larrabee traverse
A long unmarked exposed sidehill on steep talus, scree, heather and brush
Wet grass or wet rock on the sidehill is a documented no-go condition
Two 60 m gullies of loose rock with climber-triggered rockfall onto the party below
Two to four rappels on descent off aged natural tat, with at least one recorded stuck and abandoned rope
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The 6,200-6,300 ft notch on Larrabee's northwest rib is the first gate, and the South Ambo Saddle at about 6,840 ft is the second. Those two are the whole navigation of this approach and both are cols — places where the ridge is low and you can stand on the crest with ground falling away on the far side. In cloud you are counting cols, not looking at the peak.

Between them is a red talus and moraine bowl. From the notch you drop slightly into it and then climb north out of it, up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs, to the saddle. Red rock underfoot after the first col is the confirmation you are in the right bowl.

Arrival at the saddle: it is on the ridge crest directly south of the summit. Standing there, the peak is north of you and Larrabee is behind you to the south. That bearing is the check — this is not a saddle you reach with the mountain to one side.

Where the climbing actually starts is 200 yards above the saddle, not at it. From the saddle, go up the ridge crest on a faint climbers' path for roughly 200 yards, then start traversing rightward on slabby red ledges. The rock scrambling begins where the angle steepens noticeably at a distinctive rock rib: the first real move is up a small Class 3.5 cleft closely left of that rib.

De Gaulle's Nose is the aiming mark on the far side of the red face, at about 7,300 ft. The rising traverse across the red slopes goes toward it and the crossing feels very exposed. Beyond it come two 60-metre gullies with a sand-covered ledge traverse between them, and a chimney at the top of the second reached by a very airy ledge. If your route has no red traverse and no pair of long gullies, it is not this one.

And the hard condition rule: do not attempt the Larrabee sidehill on wet grass or wet rock. Parties flag that as a genuine no-go rather than a discomfort.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek off-trail to the basin under Argonaut's north face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake split and then leave it, heading up toward Argonaut's north side. There is no maintained path for this and route choice through the lower ground is yours: the terrain is swampy in places, there is a log crossing of the creek, and there is a notorious slide-alder slope that is best avoided by taking nearby talus instead.

Consistent snow generally starts around 4,700 ft. Above that, follow the drainage up toward the north face; parties have used snowshoes for much of this section.

Nothing published gives a reliable trailhead-to-base time for this approach, and the accounts that do quote figures are quoting whole days that also include a traverse of Colchuck, so no figure is given here.

The couloir above runs a constant, sustained 35-50 degrees for about 1,200 ft with no significant steps, narrowing as it goes, and exits on mid-fifth-class or icy ground onto the summit ridge system.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow climb; consistent snow starts around 4,700 ft in a normal spring
hazards: A notorious slide-alder slope on the approach, best bypassed on talus
A log crossing of Mountaineer Creek and swampy ground below the snowline
1,200 ft of sustained 35-50 degree snow with avalanche and rockfall exposure as the day warms
A mid-fifth-class or icy exit pitch
A descent involving rappels down slabs and a traverse of a wet ledge into the east gully
No maintained trail on the approach and no reliable published timing for it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The couloir that narrows is the right one. This is the most useful in-fog property of the line: it holds a constant angle for its whole length and it TAPERS, from roughly fifty feet wide at the bottom to as little as ten feet near the top. A gully that stays the same width, or that has obvious steps and pitches in it, is not this feature.

Orientation against the rock: the couloir sits immediately east of the Northeast Buttress, so from inside the couloir the buttress rock is the bounding rib on its west side. Standing at the entrance with a defined rock rib to the west and open snow slopes to the east is the correct position; standing with rock on both sides in a short, steep slot means you are in one of the minor gullies rather than the main line.

And the exit as a confirmation: this couloir does not run to the summit. It finishes with one mid-fifth-class or icy pitch onto the summit-ridge system, followed by third and fourth class scrambling to distinctive A-frame summit blocks. A line that appears to run straight to the top is a different feature.

Honest limit, stated rather than papered over: no landmark is known that distinguishes the base from neighbouring gullies at close range. The shape of the couloir and the buttress on its west are real, reliable tests; a specific arrival marker at the toe is not known and none is invented here. Scout the face from lower in the basin in good visibility before committing in the dark.

approach_variants.name: Three glaciers and two cols to the Klawatti-Austera notch, then the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near mile 20 (about 2,100 ft) and find the log crossing of the Cascade River near the Eldorado Creek confluence — it has been rebuilt repeatedly after flood damage and can be an awkward single log, so scout it before committing. On the far bank the unsigned climbers' path pushes through swampy brush and devil's club into open old growth, gains roughly 1,500 ft, then breaks onto two wide talus fields. Above them an alpine meadow leads to a slabby ramp onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and put crampons on there.

Camp at Eldorado Creek Basin around 5,600 ft, Roush Creek Basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, or push to a high camp near Eldorado's East Ridge at 7,200-7,600 ft.

From high camp the day is three miles of sustained glacier travel across three basins and two cols: the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier (crevasses worst near Eldorado's east ridge), the upper Inspiration at about 7,800 ft to Klawatti Col, then past Klawatti Peak on its left and along the upper McAllister Glacier beneath Klawatti's west face for about 0.4 mile to the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA notch at about 7,900 ft. Guide figures for that leg are roughly 1,280 ft of ascent and 592 ft of descent over 2.8 miles, about four hours one way.

Austera Peak is the high point of the Austera Towers arête rather than a separate peak, which is why the top of this climb needs as much care as the bottom.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul to Aug, while the notch is still bridged and the three glacier crossings are consolidated
hazards: Crevasse fall on all three glaciers, worse as the season progresses and bridges soften
A moat gap at the Klawatti-Austera notch that often needs stemming or a rappel of about 75 ft to reach the upper Klawatti Glacier
Route-finding in flat light or whiteout on an open ice cap with no handrail
Loose rock on every exposed rock section of the tower — the false-summit approach is explicitly loose class 3
Rime and verglas icing the final chimney even in summer
A genuinely committing and remote position with long retreat times
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the Klawatti-Austera Notch at about 7,900 ft, and you identify it by counting cols, not by looking at Austera. From the Inspiration Glacier you cross Klawatti Col first at about 7,800 ft — that one is not it. Keep Klawatti Peak on your right, follow its west face along the McAllister Glacier for about 0.4 mile, and the second break in the ridge is the one. It sits a hundred feet higher than the first.

The notch announces itself by being a problem. It is not a walk-through: a moat gap has to be stemmed or rappelled — about 75 ft — to get down onto the upper Klawatti Glacier. If you stepped through a col without having to solve anything, you are still at Klawatti Col. Old anchors have been found at the right notch; treat them as aging tat and back them up rather than as proof of position.

Above the notch, count three things in order: broken 4th-class rock off the notch, then a short cliff band that many parties bypass on scree and ledges to the right (east) rather than climbing direct, then the chockstone gully at the base of the summit tower.

The hardest thing to get right on this peak is not the base, it is the top, and the chimney is the test. Parties routinely finish on a false summit a few feet short of the true one. The true summit is reached only by crossing a narrow, exposed ridge between the two blocks and then climbing the chockstone chimney — roughly three jammed chockstones in about 60 ft, stemming and face moves on the chimney's left wall. If you have not crossed a narrow ridge and climbed a chimney, the point you are standing on is the false summit. A class 3+ ledge bypass on the peak's east side reaches the same notch without the chimney, so a party that took it has not gone wrong — but it has not confirmed its position either.

approach_variants.name: Anderson Lakes and the saddle chain to the northeast camp
approach_variants.notes: Take the Watson Lakes Trail from the road end and, at the saddle about 1.4 miles in, leave the maintained tread for a hiker's path running south along the ridge high above Lower Anderson Lake. The path opens into meadows and reaches Upper Anderson Lake — the last easy water. Leave the lake heading northeast up a short wooded gully and continue that way onto open moraine and heather slopes near 5,300 ft. Traverse under the Watson peaks and drop to about 5,000 ft to get around a buttress on their east side, then climb to a saddle at 5,360 ft and cross to the south side of the ridge. Continue east, losing a little height toward the next low point in the ridge, a saddle near 4,900 ft, crossing a short buttress on easy ledges on the way. A good camp sits at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of Bacon Peak.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: No tread, no signage and no marked line above Upper Anderson Lake
Lingering snowfields on the traverse beneath the Watson peaks
Crevasse hazard on the icecap if the line drifts onto it
Featureless snow slopes near the top — navigation in whiteout is the real difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding: The saddle sequence is the proof, and the heights go down before they go up. From the open moraine and heather at about 5,300 ft this line LOSES height twice: first to roughly 5,000 ft to get round the buttress east of the Watson peaks, then again beyond the 5,360 ft saddle, dropping toward a 4,900 ft saddle reached over a short buttress on easy ledges. A party that keeps gaining height through this stretch has stayed on the wrong side of the ridge — at the 5,360 ft saddle you cross to the south side, and remaining on the north side is the mistake. The camp lies at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of the summit, and from it the peak is gained by climbing southeast. The last test is what is under your feet: this line reaches the summit without crossing a glacier at all, so if the ground ahead is crevassed ice rather than a snow-covered slope, you have drifted onto the icecap and should rope up or come back to the walking line.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake trailhead to Couloir Camp and the North Face
approach_variants.notes:
Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near Baring; Northwest Forest Pass at the self-issue kiosk.

Leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse, not on the main trail. Follow the old abandoned logging road about a third of a mile to a cairn at roughly 2,450 ft where a rough unmaintained path splits off toward the base of the mountain. That split is easy to miss and carries no trail sign.

From the cairn the boot path climbs steep loose dirt and crosses the creek draining the face several times. Stay close to the water: the tread is faint and repeatedly lost in the brush, and the creek is the handrail. In total the lower approach fights through roughly 2,300 vertical feet of dense slide alder, vine maple and devil's club before any technical rock. Allow around seven hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear boots or sturdy approach shoes rather than carrying them.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; snow lingers in the couloir into August
hazards: Missing the unsigned cairn split at ~2,450 ft
About 2,300 ft of slide alder, vine maple and devil's club
Faint tread constantly lost in brush — losing the creek loses the line
Steep loose dirt slopes
Snow in the couloir between the ribs into August
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Couloir camp at about 4,300 ft — around 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — is the landmark that tells you which approach you are on. It is a used bivy shelf directly beneath the wall, historically the base camp for the first-ascent siege, and it remains a reasonable first night for parties splitting the approach. Above it, the ground to follow runs between two precipitous brush-and-cliff-covered rock RIBS that flank a large couloir; snow often lingers there into August, so an axe is worth having early season. Follow that ground to the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead.

Negative marker: if you have gained a ridge crest and the walking has suddenly got easier, you are on the northwest-ridge scramble line on the west side of the mountain, not on the face — the face approach never eases.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek track to the middle of the slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and the PCT about nine miles to Waptus Lake and on to a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge, roughly eleven to twelve flat miles in all. The Waptus River bridge has been out, so plan on a ford at the horse crossing.

From camp, an old, faint, unmaintained track parallels Shovel Creek through forest to a bench around 3,400 ft, then talus-hops to the base of the Mega Slab at roughly 3,700 ft.

About 19.3 km one way and 4,697 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: A long, remote approach with no confirmed reliable cell coverage
Loose rock and heavy route-finding on the Shovel Lake descent
No water on the slab itself
Deteriorating rock on the shared summit-block pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same slab, different place on it: this route takes the middle. Once you have crossed Shovel Creek off the talus and are standing under the Mega Slab, walk along the base to its middle and start there. The slab runs from about 3,700 ft at the creek to the southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft, so the middle is a real and findable place along a very long base.

The discriminator against its neighbour is a single step: Infinite Beauty starts at the LOWEST point of the slab, on a shallow rib. If you are at the bottom end of the base, you are on Infinite Beauty. Walk up along the base until you are in the middle of the sheet.

What the rock should feel like: perfect stone, mostly fourth class with occasional low-fifth moves higher up. If it is broken or vegetated you have drifted off the clean centre of the slab.

Where the two routes merge, and why that matters to the finding: both finish on the same three-pitch 5.6+ summit block. So being on the correct route matters for the first 2,000 ft and stops mattering above the shoulder. If you are already on the summit block and unsure which line you climbed, the question no longer has a practical answer.

A practical note that is part of the finding here: most parties either reverse the slab, which is easy and secure, or descend toward Shovel Lake. Reversing is the recommended option precisely because you already know that ground.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile
