bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as its neighbours and the same camp: drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then about eleven miles of trail and cross-country to a camp near 7,000 ft at the North Star-Bonanza col. It is a full day of travel and approach before anything else happens.

From camp the base is reached over talus. This route is on the west face proper rather than the north-west buttress its two neighbours share, and it tops out just right of the Southwest Summit.

It is sixteen pitches, just over 2,000 ft of net gain and about 2,800 ft of climbing, with a great deal of loose rock and several pitches where the protection is minimal and the holds are portable. Bail options near the summit roof systems are poor.

The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the only ascent on record is late August, and its two neighbours were also climbed in late summer for the driest rock
hazards: Abundant loose rock over sixteen pitches, with several pitches on minimal protection and portable holds
Poor retreat options near the summit roof systems on a wall with no fixed gear
A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight
Rock quality that varies pitch by pitch, including a choss band low on the route taken at 5.9R

Remoteness on the scale of a three-day weekend before the first pitch, on boat-and-bus access through Lucerne and Holden that has been closed since January 28, 2026 (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-05-26-04, through December 31, 2027)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first pitch begins at a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and you start just right of it. That patch is the marker the first-ascent party chose to record, and it is the only thing at the base of this wall that is a shape rather than a description. Walk the talus until you find it.

The positive test is a colour change, and it is excellent in bad light: pitch one is a 220 ft scramble at about 5.4 up white slabs to a stance below a large, steeper band of DARKER rock. White below, dark above, easy climbing. If your first pitch is hard, or if the rock is uniform, you are somewhere else.

The second confirmation is above the first: from that stance you are aiming for an obvious, large open book, which takes the second pitch at 5.8. A big open corner directly above easy white slabs is the pair of features that identifies this route. One without the other is not enough.

Left to right across this wall, facing it from the west: Oregonian, Soviet, Cascadian. This is the right-hand one — looker's right of both older routes, which are on the north-west buttress and are out of view at the far left margin of the wall from here. If you can see two other lines to your left and none to your right, you are in the correct place.

The negative marker is the strongest on this page, and it is about what lies further right: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the long snowfield, is unclimbed, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious. This route begins just right of a tiny snowpatch, not above a long one. If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.

Where it eases: difficulties relent only on reaching the ridge just south of the true summit, sixteen pitches up. There is no midway escape.

bivy.name: Snow Lakes
bivy.notes: Common base for climbing Cannon from the Snow Lakes side, about 6.5 miles up the trail; the summit day continues past Lake Viviane into the upper basin.
bivy.water: Lakes and inlet streams; filter
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (Snow zone) from May 15 to October 31
bivy.capacity: Many established sites around Upper and Lower Snow Lake

bivy.name: Nada Lake
bivy.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
bivy.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

bivy.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
bivy.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
bivy.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

approach_variants.name: East face approach to Thumbtack Rock, then the grassy gully over the divide
approach_variants.notes: Follow the Northeast Buttress and east face approach from the Alpental lot: Snow Lake trail, the Source Lake fork, then the climbers' path and snow up the broad basin running southwest toward Chair's east face. About two hours in, that basin brings you to Thumbtack Rock, the small pinnacle every route on this side uses as its landmark. At Thumbtack Rock the northwest ridge parts company with everything else. Turn right and climb a grassy gully that carries you over the ridge and around onto the northwest side, then head for the ridge itself. About 4.8 km and roughly 3,100 ft of gain from the car to the top.
approach_variants.season: Summer and autumn, once the ridge is free of snow
hazards: Poor, broken rock and runout ridge climbing — the route's own reputation is that the setting beats the climbing
A hard-to-protect move on a small vertical face of poor rock above the chockstone
Exposure on both sides of a narrow crest
A descent that goes south over false summits to find a rappel tree in the second gully east — the first gully you meet is not it
Fixed rappel gear on the descent has been found set for snow conditions and out of reach on dry rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Thumbtack Rock is the decision point, and the turn is right and up a grassy gully. Everything else on this side of the mountain continues straight on up the basin to the foot of the east face. This route is the one that leaves at the Thumbtack and crosses the divide. A published fix for the Thumbtack is 10T 0616013E 5257415N. If you are still walking up the basin under a big east face, you have gone past the turn.

The start itself is a saddle with trees on it, and the first pitch goes up the gully to the left of that saddle. Trees on a saddle, gully immediately left — that pairing is the arrival test, and both halves are visible from below in poor light.

Confirmation one pitch up, which is the strongest signal on the route: pitch one runs about 200 ft to the crest and you belay off trees on the south side of the ridge. From those trees you scramble down and left to a chimney-shaped feature with a CHOCKSTONE jammed at its top. You cannot see that chockstone from the trees; it becomes obvious as soon as you scramble across. A chockstone-capped chimney at the end of a short downward scramble means you are on the northwest ridge and nothing else.

Negative tests: if your first pitch is bolted, you are on Voie de Chaise on the east face. If you are looking up at a big buttress from the head of the basin, you never made the Thumbtack turn.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then traverse in to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the boot path drops to Early Winters Creek, crosses on logs, and climbs the timbered rib to the bench camp at 6,400-6,600 ft and on up the loose main gully to Burgundy Col.

This is the 1952 first ascent of Chianti Spire itself. The original party approached from a camp at the head of Silver Star Creek, climbed 500 ft of difficult rock to the notch between Chianti and Pernod, made a 250 ft rappel on the west face, and followed a loose gully to the Chianti-Burgundy notch, where the north face was found to hold the only route.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 200-300 ft re-ascent to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
Loose main gully below the col, with rockfall from parties above
Sand-over-slab descent above the bench, unanimously described as the worst part of the day
A short loose scramble on scree and boulders for the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway
A route with a single detailed historical account and little modern traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route starts at the notch between Chianti and Burgundy spires, and the modern way in is to traverse to it from Burgundy Col rather than to rappel into it from the west as the first ascent did. From the notch, the north face is climbed directly to the summit.

So the test is that you are in a gap between two named spires with a wall rising north of you. Burgundy on one side, Chianti on the other, and the face you are about to climb between them.

The discriminator against the peak's other lines, and it is a side-of-the-spire test: the two East Face routes are reached by descending 200-300 ft south from Burgundy Col and traversing on snow beneath Burgundy's east face until Chianti's east face comes into view. This route stops short of that, at the notch. If you are standing on snow looking at a big east-facing wall with a dihedral on its right side, you have gone past the notch and are under Rebel Yell.

And the other notch on this spire is the one at the far end: the first ascent reached the CHIANTI-PERNOD notch first, on the other side of the peak, and had to rappel 250 ft off the west face and follow a loose gully to get to this one. Two notches, one at each end of Chianti. This route uses the BURGUNDY end.

What coming back looks like, and it is the same sting the East Face routes carry: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block onto the north face, reverse the line to the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col. Firm morning snow makes that far easier than afternoon slush or bare sandy rock.

bivy.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
bivy.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
bivy.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
approach_variants.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. There is no bridge over Canyon Creek on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is unsigned, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the south shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
hazards: An unbridged Canyon Creek ford, hazardous in spring and early summer, with no fixed crossing point
Yellow paint marks that lead into a steep, loose gully rather than along the better line
Loose rock through the scramble section, reported by most parties
No water above Crater Lake
Broken glass and nails around the old lookout remains on the east peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are three markers above the lake and they come in order. First, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it. Second, at about 7,600 ft the trail ends — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three accounts agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts. Third, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping ribbon of white rock and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it. Negative marker, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight up that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line traverses across the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow arrow, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way. How you know you have finished the hard part, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ENDS well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line. There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the west — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below. Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the highest summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile east. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.

approach_variants.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it exists to avoid the Canyon Creek ford. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
hazards: A three-day committing loop with substantial cumulative gain
Same loose gully and misleading paint above
Long stretches with no bail-out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The summit end of the day is the same regardless of how you got into the basin: the trail dies around 7,600 ft into a loose gully marked by a ribbon of white rock and a yellow X, the paint leads you up rather than across, and the scrambling finishes well below the top where real trail resumes for the last quarter mile.

What differs is your bearing on arrival. Coming round by Devils Dome you meet the peak from the north-east rather than up from Crater Lake, so identify the south-ridge false top and the white ribbon from a distance before dropping into the basin, rather than expecting to walk into them off a known trail.

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.
bivy.water: glacier meltwater
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and widely rated one of the finest bivy sites in the range — granite slabs, reliable running water, and the Challenger Glacier starting at the doorstep. It is the standard last camp before roping up. Open and high, so weather arrives without warning; parties have had to navigate back down to it in fog off the glacier, which is an argument for marking it before you leave in the morning.
bivy.water: running water at the pass
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a few tents on slabs and heather

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, flat dry ground near Whatcom Pass at the end of the maintained trail and the last comfortable night of the trip — reports describe it as vastly more pleasant than anything above. This is where the route leaves trail for the Whatcom Glacier traverse, about four and a half hours and 1,750 ft of gain below Perfect Pass. Sheltered valley-head position. A knoll above the pass around 6,500 ft is also camped, with water a rock-hop away at the creek.
bivy.water: running water beside camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a party of several

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: three at a squeeze

bivy.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp

approach_variants.name: State Creek climbers' trail from the SR-20 pullout
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass. The trail leaves from the east end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.

The path drops through timber, crosses State Creek — fill up, it is the last reliable water — and then climbs steadily up into the big meadow and basin below Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half from the car to the foot of the entry gully.

Above the meadow the trail steepens into a boulder field beneath the south buttress.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: climbers' trail from the pullout is genuinely hard to find in the dark
State Creek crossing can be awkward in high spring flow
loose rock in the entry gully with parties above
the standard West Ridge descent is looser than the ascent line and has cairned traverses where the direct-looking line cliffs out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Standing in the boulder field, several large gullies come down out of the south buttress. Bear right and take the leftmost of those gullies — that specific choice is the crux of the navigation and it is where parties get it wrong, because from below the gullies look interchangeable.

Climb the gully as scrambling terrain. The place to rope up is not the bottom: continue up until you are about 100 feet from its top, where the gully FORKS and visibly steepens. That fork is the marker. Pitch one goes up the left side of the gully from there to gain the ridge crest. If you rope up down at the base you burn time on ground everybody scrambles; if you find yourself topping out of a gully with no fork and no steepening, you are in the wrong one.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, then east along the ledge and up a long steep hillside — around 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge to the rock.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close annually for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep approach hillside
Steep, coarse granite with few moderates
Northwest aspect — shaded and cold in the morning
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up and right from Logger's Ledge, the left side of Midnight Rock is what you meet first. Midnight is the tall wall — about 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, coarse granite with parallel-sided cracks — and it faces northwest, so it is shaded through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime, alongside, has almost nothing on it. Before hunting along the ground for a start, note that several of Midnight's lines begin from the enormous ledge crossing the middle of the CENTRE of the wall, reached by first climbing Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting or Wasp — so a route you cannot find at deck level may not have a deck-level start at all. No source consulted for this pass records this route's own start position; confirm against a topo.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
the 2002 avalanche swath at about 4,500 ft where the trail is destroyed
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log
open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
unmarked cross-country traverse if the cairns are lost
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with CAIRNS and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately north of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is correct and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

approach_variants.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
approach_variants.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

approach_variants.name: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,100 ft — the first ten miles paved, the rest rough gravel and high-clearance recommended. Hike the Eldorado climbers' trail through forest, cross the creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft, roughly four miles and 6,000 ft of gain.

From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the col between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle at about 7,600 ft. That col is the base.

Most parties take eight to twelve hours round trip from high camp, and descend by the Northwest Ridge rather than reversing this line — which means the day ends on unfamiliar ground with rappels and a moat, so scout the Northwest Ridge's top as you pass it.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once glacier bridges and moats have stabilised but before the early-season storms return
hazards: Crevasse-fall potential on the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
Loose, thinly protectable rock on the first pitch off the col — test every placement
A bottomless moat on the glacier traverse partway up the route, where the line steps off the ridge and back on
A complex, easy-to-misroute Northwest Ridge descent with moat and rappel-anchor hazards at the end of a long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a named col: the one between Point 8386 and Dorado Needle, at about 7,600 ft. The climbing starts immediately off it — steep, exposed mid-fifth moves straight from the col, no walk-in. If you had to travel further along the glacier after crossing a col before you found rock, you are at the wrong col.

The first pitch identifies itself by being nasty and by carrying a marker: it is a loose, poorly protectable 5.5, and A horn with an existing sling sits about 100 ft up. Loose rock plus a slung horn a rope-length up is the confirmation.

There is an alternative start and it has its own landmark: a line beneath the 'cannonball hole' to the right avoids that first loose section, at the cost of a moat crossing. A hole in the rock you could name is not a feature you find by accident — if you can see it, you are in the right place and you have a choice to make.

Tell it from its neighbours by length and by difficulty, because all four routes on this needle are different sizes. This one is longer and a bit harder than the Northwest Ridge (three short pitches from a small col at the top of the McAllister apron) and easier than the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from a gully 700 ft below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass). It follows the CENTRE portion of the rock on an obvious ridge line.

The route steps off the ridge partway up and that is expected, not an error: after several ropelengths of class 3-4 you descend into a notch, traverse the glacier, and regain the ridge at a ledge marked by quartzite bands. Watch for a bottomless moat there. Pale banded rock on a ledge is the marker to aim for.

And the finish is countable: two short rappels drop into the notch below the true summit, then two sustained 5.7 crack pitches to the top. If you have climbed one hard pitch and stood on a summit, you were on the sub-summit tower.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake to the toe of the nordwand
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

In the winter and spring conditions most parties come for, this is a much bigger undertaking than the summer figure suggests: expect snowshoes or skis, real avalanche exposure, and most parties camping at the lake rather than trying it car-to-car. Allow three to five hours from the lake to the base depending on the snowpack.

From the lake, work up talus and snow along the moraine beneath the north face. Move as a rope team across the apron below the wall — the overhead rock and icefall hazard is the reason.
approach_variants.season: Summer as a rock route; late winter and spring for ice and mixed, which is how it is usually climbed now
hazards: Overhead rock and icefall on the apron below the face — move as a rope team
Avalanche exposure on the winter and spring approach
800 ft of simul-climbing before any belayed pitch
Long approach from the lake under snow (3-5 hours)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Gerber-Sink takes the LOWEST point of Dragontail's north wall. That is the whole test, and it is a thing you can see rather than a distance you have to pace out.

Standing on the moraine, find the point where the talus and snow apron runs highest into the rock — the toe of the face. Triple Couloirs starts further left (west) of it and Backbone Ridge with its Fin is further right (east); Gerber-Sink is the line between them, out of the toe. In winter conditions the easiest entry is just to the right of the toe of the face.

Higher up, the feature that confirms the line is the dome or tower sitting between Backbone's Fin and the tower at the foot of the third of the Triple Couloirs — the route traverses across it. If the feature above you is one of those two towers rather than the dome between them, you are on the wrong side of the correct line.

One inverted marker worth knowing: the first 800 ft or so is low-angle simul-climbing before you reach the rock band where the technical climbing starts. Easy ground at the bottom is correct here and is not evidence that you are off route.

bivy.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows
bivy.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.
bivy.water: Bean Creek runs through the basin and is the reason the camp is here, but it is a small east-side creek and by late August only one of the several channels may still be running. The dependable fill is lower down, where the trail crosses Bean Creek at the split with the Earl Peak branch — top off there rather than assuming the basin will provide, and assume nothing at all above the basin, because the climb to Earl Pass and the whole southwest ridge are dry.
bivy.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
bivy.capacity: A stand of trees at the edge of the meadow holds four or more multi-tent sites, and there are scattered singles beyond it; two or three parties fit comfortably and it fills on summer weekends. No toilet of any kind.

bivy.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
bivy.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
bivy.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
bivy.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is PROHIBITED anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Eye Col
approach_variants.notes: From the basin camp below Mount Terror around 6,050 ft, head west and drop about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek. Traverse north through Crescent Creek Basin, keeping the party together through the scree to limit rockfall and hugging the cliffs, then make a rising traverse beneath the Eye Col gully that carries you past an adjacent buttress rather than straight up at it. The notch at about 7,400 ft is reached by continuing past a gully that would otherwise force a rappel — that decoy gully is the thing to walk by. The last stretch to the col is scree you walk up rather than rock you climb.
approach_variants.season: Mid Jul-early Sep
hazards: Constantly falling rock in the Eye Col gully
Steep, loose gully climbing with genuine route-finding uncertainty on this south side
Disorienting in cloud or low light — the south side carries comparatively sparse route information
A multi-day committing approach over The Barrier before any of this begins
approach_variants.baseFinding: Chockstones are the gate, and the view through the col is the confirmation. Going up toward the Eye Col, the small chockstones low in the gully present no real problem and are scrambled past; higher, the LARGER chockstones put the ground into fifth class, and that size change is where the rope comes out. If you are still stepping over rubble you are low; if you are stemming past a jammed block you are at the transition. The Eye Col itself is the notch between East and West Twin Needle at about 7,400 ft, gained on scree from the south, and it announces itself: from it you get your first sight through the gap to the Northern Pickets, and East Twin Needle stands directly above it. Know which line you intend before you leave the col — the Eye Col sits on the west side of East Twin Needle, while the peak's hard, tremendously exposed east arete is on the opposite flank and is reached along the ridge from the east, not from here.

bivy.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
bivy.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first three and a half miles are relentless forest switchbacks with nothing to drink. Stopping here makes the second day the good one. Note that the climbers' line for Elephant Butte does not continue to the lookout at all — it leaves this trail at an unmarked junction somewhere around four thousand three hundred to four thousand four hundred feet and turns north up the ridge crest west of the creek. No elevation is recorded for the camp because no confident figure was found. Both this camp and the trail it sits on have been closed by fire for most of the last three years; confirm before planning around it.
bivy.water: Sourdough Creek runs at the camp and is the first water on the whole climb from Diablo — the lower trail has essentially none. Early in the season the crossing can be bridged by snow, which is worth treating with care rather than walking onto.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, collected at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing process. This is a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night rather than open ground, so a walk-up can be refused. A bear canister is required here through the main season; the park lends them free at the permit desk. No fires. Pets are not allowed at the camp.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots only, with a hard limit of four people on the site. That is the smallest party cap of anything on this approach and it rules the camp out for a larger group entirely.

bivy.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
bivy.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in the corridor reachable in winter — a late-March overnight on continuous snow is a known way to do the ridge, with the caveat that spring sun softens the slopes badly by mid-morning. For a summer ascent of the butte it is a detour, since the climbers' line leaves the trail well below the lookout and never comes here. It also carries the same warning as everything else: the trail, both designated camps, and the Sourdough and Elephant Butte zones have all been closed by an active fire in the drainage, on top of an earlier fire that shut the trail for two and a half years before it briefly reopened. Check the closure status first; it is the single thing most likely to end this trip.
bivy.water: Melted snow in the cold months, which is when this site makes sense. In summer there is nothing at the summit and the tarns further along the ridge are the supply.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Sourdough cross-country zone: six people per party, six parties a night, walk-up only. The lookout building is closed and camping is not permitted at it, so the site is the open ground near the top rather than the structure. Same durable-surface, no-fire and no-meadow rules as the rest of the zone.
bivy.capacity: Open ground near the summit, a small party at a time. In winter and spring it is a snow camp with no defined pitch at all.

bivy.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
bivy.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went for the summit from there. It is still a long way: from the ridge high point the ground drops something like fifteen hundred feet before you regain that and another thousand to the top, and a full trip is closer to twenty miles and ten thousand feet of gain and loss over two nights. Several strong parties have reached the ridge in a single push and turned round because the butte was still too far. The north-east side of the crest is very steep, so stay on it or just south-west of it. Snow-free is roughly late July into September, which is unhelpfully the same window in which the water disappears.
bivy.water: Small tarns and snowmelt ponds scattered over the ridge — plentiful in late June, and the single best reason to come early. They do dry. By August in a warm year parties report water on the ridge becoming a real problem, and which pools survive latest is not documented anywhere reliable. Late in the season carry enough to camp dry.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. There is no Stetattle Ridge zone — the ridge falls between the Sourdough zone and the Elephant Butte zone, and your permit has to name the one you will actually sleep in. Both allow a party of six and six parties a night. Neither is reservable in advance: they are walk-up zones, issued in person, with a share of the allocation held for same-day and next-day pickup. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow pockets that make the ridge look inviting, and not within a hundred feet of a tarn. No fires in a cross-country zone. Waste in a cathole, or carried out on snow and bare rock. A canister is not formally required in these two zones, but the ridge is open ground with nothing to hang from, so bring one anyway.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country ground rather than sites. Small grassy pockets and gravel benches recur the length of the ridge, easily enough for the zone's limit of six parties, and no two accounts stop in the same place.

bivy.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
bivy.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at walking-to-scrambling ground. The east ridge is a different proposition entirely and has been described by a party crossing it on a long Picket traverse as among the hardest ground of that whole trip, needing roped downclimbs and rappels — so do not read the easy summit as an easy mountain from every side. The named benches near the pass east of the butte belong to the traverse route rather than to this approach, and a party coming from Stetattle Ridge will not pass them. No elevation is recorded: no account that slept on this shoulder coming from Stetattle Ridge stated one, and the figures published for the traverse-side benches describe different ground.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small pools, entirely seasonal. There is no dependable source and nothing to plan on. Fill on the ridge before committing to the descent toward the butte.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Elephant Butte cross-country zone: six people maximum, six parties a night, walk-up only from Marblemount. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail and out of sight of both, which up here is automatic. Durable surfaces only, no fires, waste packed out above treeline.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no name. Parties travelling the crest report finding flat ground on the shoulder and on the benches near the pass east of the peak, tight enough that three tents felt crowded. Treat it as somewhere you stop, not somewhere you book.

wa_enchantment_enchainment.beta: Peak order and exact lines are up to the party; the loop below runs west to east. STUART: from the Stuart Lake valley climb slopes toward Long Pass, then steep snow to a notch at about 7,950 ft on the northwest face; drop slightly, traverse snow to a gully that shortcuts onto the upper West Ridge (continuous snow early season, with 3rd class rock beside it), then follow the West Ridge to the summit. The West Ridge is a notorious route-finding trap that benights parties climbing it for the first time, so know the line before you go. SHERPA: descend the upper Cascadian Couloir and cut east to the Stuart-Sherpa col (a short 4th class downclimb on the way), then climb Sherpa's West Ridge, keeping left of the steeper cracks on easier ground. Leave Sherpa by the north side: a short 4th/5th class downclimb, then trend skier's left through a scrambly gully to a large vegetated ledge near 8,100 ft, and on down a broader gully to about 7,200 ft. Sherpa to Argonaut: a long, time-consuming traverse across high granite slabs and goat paths to Argonaut's south-side gullies; the alternative is to drop to the valley trail and climb back up. ARGONAUT: ascend the southern gullies on easy ground to just below the east ridge, with a short easy-fifth-class step to the summit; descend by rappel down the east face. Colchuck and Dragontail: gain the Colchuck-Dragontail col and tag each summit by its scramble from the col, then descend to Aasgard Pass. The Core: from Aasgard Pass continue into the upper Enchantment basin for Little Annapurna (a walk-up from the basin), McClellan Peak (loose scrambling), then Enchantment Peak via Prusik Pass (talus, with a 4th class summit pillar; it has two summits of similar height, so tag both if in doubt) and finally Cannon Mountain from the Enchantment side.

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, then a long ledge traverse across the face
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the highway turnout about two miles east of Washington Pass, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. Nothing is signed.

The climbers' path drops steeply from the west end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked here and there by cairns, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs, and climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation. The old line finishes with two or three informal fixed ropes across an avalanche path; a newer variation bears right just before them and needs only a little scrambling.

This route sees very few ascents, so current conditions beta effectively does not exist and there will be no traffic to follow. Budget the extra time the traverse costs on top of the walk in.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and approach snow have gone
hazards: The base is a 250-yard third and fourth-class traverse away from the obvious start
Very few ascents, so no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information
The crux comes off a belay high on the route in thin cracks with sparse protection; knifeblades and thin pins are useful
Dirty and vegetated cracks in places
Descent is by the neighbouring route's rappels or its loose gully, not by reversing this line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You do not start where the path ends. Arrive first at the base of the formation's trade route — identified by tree snags on the left as the ground steepens, before the gully. From there, traverse about two hundred and fifty yards across the face on third and fourth-class ledges, finishing just right of centre on the north-west face. That traverse is the approach to this climb and it is the piece everyone underestimates.

The test that you have gone far enough is the first pitch itself. It is a hundred-foot chimney and hand crack ending on a large ledge, and it is easy — around 5.4. If the ground in front of you is steep or technical at the very start, you have stopped short. A hundred feet of easy chimney to a big ledge is the signature.

Confirm on the pitches above, because the low ground is not distinctive. Pitch two is a slightly vegetated hands-and-fists corner. Pitch three follows the same corner then breaks right on thin face climbing to a ledge with a cave. Pitch four is finger cracks to a large slabby ledge. Corner, then a cave ledge, then a slabby ledge: that sequence is the line.

Negative markers, and both are easy to fall into. If you racked up at the snags and started climbing without traversing, you are on the trade route — much easier, and it will feel like it. If your first pitch is protected by BOLTS, you are on the partly bolted four-pitch line beside the gully; this route's first pitch has no bolts, and its only fixed hardware is higher up — two bolted belays and a single bolt at the crux.

Be warned that the line is not continuously natural and some cracks are dirty and vegetated. That is the character of the route rather than evidence you are off it. The crux comes late, right off a belay high on the climb, in very thin cracks with sparse protection.

At the top it joins the trade route for its final scrambly ridge pitches, and the descent is that route's line: rappel it, or take the third-class gully on climbers' right, which is faster and loose.

approach_variants.name: Glacier Basin Trail to the timbered ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Monte Cristo townsite take the Glacier Basin Trail — not the Poodle Dog Pass trail, which leaves the townsite southward toward Silvertip and Columbia and does not reach Foggy Peak at all. Follow it about a mile and a half, a short distance above the falls, and leave it near 4,200 ft at the point where Glacier Creek is easy and brush-free to reach; that is the last reliable water. There are two traverses on this route with a climb between them, and collapsing them into one is how parties get it wrong. First, cross the creek and traverse nearly level to the base of the timbered ridge. Then climb that ridge — start on its right where there is less brush and shift onto its left side after several hundred feet to avoid small cliff bands, where a game trail helps — carrying on up to anywhere between about 4,800 and 5,300 ft. Lower means more brush, higher means gain you give straight back, and 5,100 ft is the usual compromise. Only then turn left for the second, near-level traverse.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Brushy sidehill traversing, and small cliff bands on the timbered ridge
Conditions at the gully entrance vary enormously by month — one party met ice-hard snow with deep moats on the right and huge overhangs on the left
The summit gully is steep with abundant loose, downsloping rock — helmets, and do not climb directly beneath one another
Real exposure on the short final scramble off the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding: The only ridge in the area with large trees on it, then a cliffy nuisance ridge. Cross Glacier Creek above the falls and traverse nearly level to the base of a timbered ridge — unmistakable, because it is the only rib on this slope carrying big trees while everything either side of it is brush and talus. That ridge is the first landmark and it is CLIMBED, not skirted. The second comes at the end of the upper traverse near 5,100 ft: a cliffy ridge that has to be got around rather than crossed. Once past it, turn right and go straight up the talus slopes toward the summit gully. At the gully entrance the season decides the day — in a good year the snowfield runs continuously into the gully, and where it has pulled back, the rock immediately to its left has gone at short class 4. The gully above is mostly class 3 and finishes at a notch on the skyline just west of the true summit; aim for that notch, not for the summit block. A gully topping out at the summit, or east of it, is the wrong one.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp

approach_variants.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
approach_variants.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.
approach_variants.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
hazards: A moat where the snow pulls back from the rock guards the top of the couloir. Expect a short steep step or a band of loose rock to get over it, and expect it to be worse the later in the season you go.
Rockfall once the sun reaches the couloir — parties above are the usual source, so it pays to be off it early.
40–50° snow near the top, on ground where a slip does not stop on its own.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The notch is the low point on the skyline between Forbidden and Mount Torment, at 8,265 ft, and the couloir below it is the obvious continuous snow line splitting the left-hand edge of the south face. Navigate to the notch, not to the first gully you reach — several lines start off the same snowfield and only this one tops out at the crest. You are at the base of the climbing when you step through the notch onto the ridge crest; from there the route to the summit runs to climber's right.

approach_variants.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
approach_variants.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
hazards: Loose rock from bottom to top. Keep the party out of one another's fall line rather than spread across the gully.
The parallel gullies are easy to confuse, and committing to the wrong one puts you on the ridge away from the notch with loose ground to traverse back.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cat Scratch is not the snow couloir, and that mix-up is the usual reason parties lose time here: it is the parallel rock gully system just west (climber's left) of the couloir, and it tops out at the same 8,265 ft notch. Several parallel gullies in that system look alike from below — the correct one finishes at the notch itself rather than on the ridge either side of it, so pick your line by where it ENDS on the skyline, not by which entrance looks easiest from the basin.

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.notes:
Distance is one-way horizontal; almost all of the effort is vertical. From I-90 Exit 34 at North Bend, drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR 56) east — paved, then good gravel — staying on FR 56 past the Taylor River Road (FR 5620) junction, about 2.6 miles further, to a wide gravel wash and old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road at roughly 1,150-1,200 ft.

There is no maintained or numbered Forest Service trail here. This is an unmaintained climbers' boot path with intermittent cairns and pink flagging.

From the wash, follow the dry creekbed uphill for roughly a mile. A boot path exits climber's left into second-growth forest with light brush before the creek narrows. Several boot-path branches exist low down: avoid the flat, early traverse that cuts across to the slab too low, and take the higher up-and-down traverse instead.

At about 2,200 ft the path enters a loose dirt-and-scree gully mixed with vegetation — unpleasant, roughly 400 ft of gain — then exits climber's left onto a wooded ridge for another 400 ft of steep but relatively brush-free ground. There is no reliable water past the creek near the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, and only in bone-dry conditions
hazards: No water above the trailhead creek
About 40-degree loose duff above the slab; huckleberry stems are the handholds
Slabs and dirt gullies become treacherous when even slightly wet
Braided boot paths low down leading to the slab at the wrong height
Loose and mossy rock in #2 Gully
Serious route-finding above the slab — intermittent path, cairns and flagging only
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the first major slab at about 2,900 ft, roughly an hour and 1,700 ft above the car. It is unmistakable by contrast: it is the first clean rock of the day after nothing but duff, dirt and scree. Two low-fifth pitches follow intersecting DIKES up it; parties either solo them or rope up.

The negative marker is the dirt gully. If you have arrived at slab without first grovelling through the loose dirt-and-scree gully at about 2,200 ft, you took the low flat traverse and you are on the slab too far along — traverse up and left to regain the line. Above the slab the landmarks come in a fixed order and that order is how you confirm you are still on it: dirt and heather above the slab's upper-left edge, a tiny notch, a knife-edge razorback, and then a flat bivy clearing known as the glade saddle. A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20 ft scramble step follows, then a rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse leading to the Y Notch, where the line joins the gully locally called #2 Gully — loose rock on one side, polished mossy rock on the other — for the last 600 ft or so to the summit ridge at 5,519 ft.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then the Foam Creek high traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Sauk River trailhead at about 2,050 ft, take Trail #649 up the valley and then the steep switchbacks to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, roughly nine miles in.

Rather than dropping into the basin, continue east on the Foam Creek trail for about two miles, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, and traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending north-east to Glacier Gap at about 7,250 ft — where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet, and the standard high camp.

Summit day from Glacier Gap is short in distance but has intermediate descent in it as well as gain: gentle snow above camp, then a climbers' track over volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: rockfall corridor below Disappointment Peak on the traverse
crevasses on the Gerdine and Cool glaciers
loose volcanic scree on the connecting ground
long approach with no maintained trail above White Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Glacier Gap is confirmed the same way as for the cleaver — it is the col where two glaciers meet, not a saddle with ice on one side only.

This route deliberately AVOIDS the fourth-class ground: the line skirts Disappointment Peak by staying on the upper edges of the Gerdine and then the Cool. So the test that you are on the right variation is that you are on snow and scree the whole way, working around the peak rather than over it. If you are scrambling rock and gaining a summit, you have drifted onto the direct line over Disappointment Peak.

On the Cool Glacier expect to end-run one or two crevasses before rejoining the climbers' track for the final steep pitch to the summit — that track, worn into scree and snow by traffic, is the most reliable confirmation you are on the standard line, so look for it rather than for a feature.

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: Emergency only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
approach_variants.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
hazards: An upper glacier described by parties as a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses that needs deliberate, slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left beneath the Kennedy Peak wall, where some parties have had to belay off bare glacier ice
Trading crevasse navigation for rockfall by hugging the left wall — the simplification is real and so is the cost
A bergschrund at the head of the glacier whose only crossing may be a single bridge found from the snow dome above it
8,200 ft of gain from a trailhead served by a road that has been closed at milepost 3.7, so the walk in may be far longer than the mileage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climb is below you, not above you, and that is the whole test. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go down off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

Arrival: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep right; on the upper glacier take the CENTRE. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

The discriminator against Frostbite Ridge, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and KENNEDY glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the ridge. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

The top end, and it is a real decision point: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing left to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay left of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

What hugging the left wall costs: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.

bivy.name: 5,500 ft bivy below the slabs
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most commonly used one on this side of the peak. Reached after the slide-alder section and a crossing of the creek, tucked just below the low-angle slabs with rock walls around it and running water on hand. Nothing above it is comfortable, and the slabs above lead straight onto the glacier in the morning.
bivy.water: the creek right at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: about four people

bivy.name: Goode Glacier toe
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the moraine and rubble between roughly 6,400 and 6,800 ft. Flat ground is genuinely limited and the good spots are specific rather than general — expect to hunt for them, and expect glacier noise all night.
