It is the highest planned camp and the one that makes the couloir a reasonable day, but the water problem is real by late summer.
bivy.water: scarce near camp late season; fill at the last reliable stream below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: limited — a small number of usable flat spots, not a big-party site

bivy.name: 5,200 ft camp to the west
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the fallback if you run out of daylight in the brush below. Perfectly serviceable, but reports consistently say the extra three hundred feet up to the higher bivy is worth carrying, because summit day from here is long enough already.
bivy.water: creek nearby
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: West Tower ledge, upper mountain
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp. A narrow shelf on the north side of the crest between the West Tower and the main summit, where a solo climber spent a night wedged between rocks and still lost sleep to constant south wind. No water, no flat ground worth the name, and a serious place to be caught. It exists, and that is the only reason to know about it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: Lateral moraine camp above Goode Glacier

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
approach_variants.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do not take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends left up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
Log-jam crossing of the creek is slick and runs high in spring
The fork near the exposed rock band around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet is a known route-finding trap; the outcrop ahead is not the way
Loose rock on the talus fan and at the ramp
No reliable water above the creek and the waterfall ravine in late summer
Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus; route-finding rather than difficulty is the main hazard here
Multiple search-and-rescue incidents have occurred on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt a cliff band and boulder-hop up the talus fan toward the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face. The base of the technical ground is the top of that fan — and the feature you are looking for cannot be seen from below. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and only appears once you are underneath it, which is exactly why parties overshoot by continuing up the rockslide. The unmistakable test is the single step at the ramp's foot: a boulder with two options off it, a left-hand line past a CHOCKSTONE that takes a steep low-fifth move, and a right-hand line, steeper and more exposed but on solid holds, which is what most parties take. If there is no boulder with a two-way step above it, you are not at the ramp. Negative marker: if you are still grinding up loose rockslide with no ramp cutting off to either side, you have gone past the entry — the ramp is entered from the talus, not from the top of it. Higher up, the next landmark is a keyhole notch through the ridge to the north side; if you have not passed the ramp step you will not reach it.

approach_variants.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
approach_variants.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented wrong turn in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
approach_variants.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir tops out at the same saddle as the summer line, so the base of the climbing is identical: drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt the cliff band, then boulder-hop up the talus fan to the upper tree benches below the south face. The ramp at the top of the fan is invisible until you are under it; identify it by the boulder at its foot with a two-way step above — a left-hand chockstone move at low fifth, or a steeper, more exposed line on good holds to the right. Negative marker: if you are still on snow when you expect to be on talus, you have carried on above the saddle into the wrong basin; the couloir delivers you to a saddle, and the talus fan starts on the far side of it.

bivy.name: Chikamin-Dome col
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one most parties use for Gunsight — an established site on the col reached by roping up at Itswoot Pass and crossing the Dome Glacier. Room is genuinely tight: one party spent half an hour of earthwork levelling ground for a four-person tent. It is a col, so it funnels wind, but it is reported as the sheltered option compared with the open glacier either side. Everything here is melted, so carry fuel accordingly.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a small tent or several bivy sacks; a four-person tent needs building out

bivy.name: Bachelor Flats / Bachelor Meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the standard first night after leaving maintained trail at the Bachelor Creek crossing. An informal but heavily used forest camp in a clearing — sheltered, buggy, and low. Most parties stop here because the unmaintained climbers' path above eats time and the day from the car is already long.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek
bivy.capacity: multiple tents in the clearing

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp in heather meadow past Cub Pass, and the busiest ground on the approach — a summer weekend has been described with a dozen or more parties spread through these meadows and several more on Itswoot Ridge above. Comfortable and well watered, but it leaves the glacier travel and the col for the following day.
bivy.water: Cub Lake and its outlet

bivy.name: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
bivy.notes: PLANNED advanced camp, about ninety minutes of descending traverse below the col and directly under Gunsight's west face. Parties move here to shorten summit day rather than day-climbing from the col. It is a glacier bench: rope up moving to and from it, site the tent clear of the fall line off the face, and expect a cold, fully exposed pitch.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: small — a snow dome and rock outcrop, a tent or two

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ladder of landmarks above the basin is what fixes your position, and they come in order. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - if your gully has no chockstone bottleneck in it, you are in the wrong drainage and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

From camp the base of the route is another thousand feet or so above, gained on slabs and connecting gullies. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

Check which summit is above you. This route is on the south peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the south of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

And check that you left the trail at all. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrival changes, the approach does not. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

The markers are the same ladder, in the same order: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

The summit test still applies. This route is on the south peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The departure from the trail is just beyond Willow Lake, and the lake is the marker. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

From there the ground is the test rather than any tread: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching MEADOWS near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

Above the meadows the cliff bands are bypassed, not climbed. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

The arrival is a saddle at about 6,200 ft directly beneath the buttress on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. If you have arrived somewhere with running water, you are not there yet. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of this climb is a fork, and the fork is marked by a rock formation called the Thumb. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to Mount Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to Inner Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

The fog test that does not need the Thumb, and it is the better one, is the shape of the gully you end up in. From the broad couloir, veer right into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled defile. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

Second test, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

What going too far looks like, and it is the recorded way this route goes wrong: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the southwest summit, which has no easy connection across to the true northeast high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

Safety note that is part of the route-finding: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Crystal Pass the base of the climb is directly below you rather than above you, which is the one real advantage of this side. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the right (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

The test is still the Thumb and the defile, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that NARROWS to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the right side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

The fog test for that northeast line is which side of the crest you are on. Stay on the crest's right-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

What going too far looks like: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the southwest summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the northeast top.

Honest limit: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail, take the right branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Iron Horse sits in the tight cluster with Sagittarius and Numbah Ten and shares an anchor with Sagittarius.

The reliable marker is its neighbour: Numbah Ten is the BOLTED dihedral immediately left of Iron Horse, and the obvious groove at the base of that dihedral belongs to Numbah Ten and Amandla, not to this. Step right off that groove.

Japanese Gardens is further right again, starting midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla.

bivy.name: Crater Creek Meadows bench
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard staging point for the south face, on a heather bench above Crater Creek northwest of point 7001. Reached in roughly eight hours and eleven miles from the car, after the Jerry Glacier traverse and the drop into Crater Creek Basin. Parties choose it over Jerry Lakes specifically because it shortens the summit day onto the face. Terrain gives moderate wind shelter. Permit status is not confirmed for this basin — check the zone before you go.
bivy.water: Crater Creek, about 200 ft below camp
bivy.capacity: small — comfortable for a party of two

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, a grassy boulder-strewn bowl with several separate sites; the best of them sits by the small lake between the two large ones. Snow-free by mid-August. It is the more pleasant camp of the two and the obvious stop if you arrive late, but it leaves a longer traverse to the face on summit day. Open bowl, so afternoon wind. Fire-scarred forest on the approach into the basin. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: four alpine lakes
bivy.capacity: multiple parties across the basin

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes Peak south saddle
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — on record only as an unplanned night out, sat through in a bivy sack and an emergency blanket with little wind protection and a cold, sleepless result. Worth knowing exists if a party is caught on the ridge between the lakes and the Crater Mountain saddle, and worth planning not to use.
bivy.water: none at the saddle

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp

approach_variants.name: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,150 ft, then the standard Eldorado climbers' path: forest, boulder field, treeline, and camps in Eldorado Basin / Roush Creek around 6,000-6,300 ft. Climb the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge near 7,500 ft, then traverse roughly a mile and a half north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft.

Klawatti Col is not the start of this route. Continue past it, along a lobe of the McAllister Glacier under Klawatti Peak's west face, about 0.4 mile to the next break in the ridge — the Klawatti-Austera Col at about 7,900 ft. The scramble takes about an hour from that col, up to two hours if you count from Klawatti Col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, when the crest and the connecting cols are snow-free enough to scramble
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration and the upper McAllister lobe
A moat at the Klawatti-Austera col that ranges from class 4 to class 5 depending on where you cross it
Exposure on narrow sections of the crest, where route-finding is what keeps the grade at third class
Loose rock on the ledge traverses around The Smokestack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Count the cols: you want the second one. Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft is where the peak's other two routes start; this route starts at the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA col at about 7,900 ft, a further 0.4 mile north along the foot of Klawatti's west face and a hundred feet higher.

The second col identifies itself by being a problem, and it offers a choice of two crossings — which is itself the confirmation. Receding snow leaves a moat here. The LOWEST notch is class 5 downclimbing; a crossing to the right (southeast) of the lowest notch is class 4. Parties have also found an old rappel anchor at this col and used it. A col you walked over without choosing between two ways down is Klawatti Col, one short.

Gain the lower ridge on its east side — the crest itself is harder than it needs to be low down, and the east flank is the easy way onto it.

The Smokestack is the confirming landmark and it is unmistakable. Class 3 scrambling up the crest brings you to a rock tower around 8,400 ft that the route is named around. You do not climb it: go round it on its west side by a short gully and regain the crest above. A party that has climbed a tower on the ridge rather than walked around it has gone off route. A party that reached the summit without ever passing a tower was never on the North Ridge.

Negative test for the other direction: if the ground in front of you is a snow face rather than a ridge crest, you are below the south-facing snow line and one col too far south.

What is thin here, said plainly: this ridge is barely written up. The col elevations, the Smokestack and the east-side start come from the route's own record; the detail about the two crossings at the moat and the old anchor comes from accounts that could not be retrieved in full, so treat the crossing description as a warning to expect a choice rather than as a promise about which side is easier this year.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado ice cap to Klawatti Col, then the buttress that stands directly above camp
approach_variants.notes: The whole approach is the Eldorado one: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the river crossing, the steep unmaintained boot path through old growth to the boulder field, and up into Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek basin. Camp there or push on to the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,500-7,600 ft. From that camp the day is glacier travel, not a trail. Rope up, cross the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit, and continue north-northeast to Klawatti Col at about 7,800 ft, the saddle dividing the Klawatti and McAllister glaciers on Klawatti Peak's south side. This traverse is the navigational crux of the whole route — it is flat, featureless and whiteouts are routine, so carry a bearing or a track and be prepared to navigate blind. Parties commonly camp at the col itself. Three Klawatti routes leave from cols within half a mile of each other. A wilderness permit for the Klawatti zone comes from the Marblemount ranger station.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the Inspiration Glacier traverse and the moat at the foot of the buttress are reliably crossable
hazards: Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers, worst near Eldorado's east ridge
Whiteout navigation on a flat, featureless ice cap with no handrail
A moat at the foot of the buttress where the glacier has pulled back from the rock
Rock repeatedly described as lousy and loose — test every hold rather than trusting the grade
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The buttress stands directly above the Klawatti camp and is minutes from it — not a traverse away. That is the first thing that separates it from the peak's other two routes. If you have walked more than a few minutes from the saddle you have started the wrong climb.

The deciding test is what is above the moat, and it is a one-look test. Cross the moat and the ground above is rock and keeps being rock: two or three short low-fifth pitches, then class 4, then scrambling. If there are several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow above a short rock step, you are on the south-facing snow line known as the southeast face, which starts from the same col and is a snow climb with one rock move rather than a rock climb. That difference decides whether you needed a rack or a second tool.

The third route is at a different col entirely. The North Ridge starts from the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA col at about 7,900 ft, roughly 0.4 mile further along under Klawatti's west face — a separate notch a hundred feet higher, and one you have to solve rather than walk through. If you are walking a ridge crest north with a rock tower ahead of you, you have gone past this route to that one.

What the col looks like: a broad saddle with usable bivy sites on the south side, and the low point between the Klawatti Glacier on one side and the McAllister on the other — so from it you can see down both. A spot where the ground only falls away one way is not the col.

bivy.name: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
bivy.notes: The climbing camp for KOLOLO PEAKS, and the reason Kololo is a three-day trip rather than a weekend scramble. It sits in the stark rock-and-snow basin on the edge of what remains of the White Chuck Glacier, reached from the North Fork Sauk road end by twelve or thirteen miles of walking — the long river approach, then the steep switchbacking climb to White Pass, then east on the crest trail and out along the Foam Basin path toward Foam Pass. Eight hours from the road to camp is a normal rather than a slow time for a party carrying overnight gear. From here the peaks themselves are straightforward, a walk on glacier remnant and snow followed by easy scrambling on rubbly volcanic rock, and moving from one summit to the next is simple. The glacier is the thing to understand: it has retreated further and faster than almost anything in the range and much of what maps show as ice is now bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds, with the surviving ice thin, hard and holed by open crevasses late in the season. That means crampons rather than a snow plod by September, and it means route descriptions written twenty years ago describe a surface that is gone. Lower camps on the same approach sit at the river bench, at White Pass and at the gap above this basin. Exposed ground with no shelter, confusing in fog, and a long way from help.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams and ponds through the basin, running all through the climbing season and often silty. Late in a hot summer the flow drops to a trickle off the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time. Everybody camped here drinks it, so site the toilet well away from it.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free self-issue permit collected at the North Fork Sauk trailhead box, twelve-person party limit. No fires: this is bare rock, pumice and snow above treeline with nothing to burn and nothing that recovers. Human waste is carried out or buried properly well away from the meltwater. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
bivy.capacity: Open bare-ground bivouac sites scattered through the basin, with room for several parties and no crowding — this is a big, empty place. Rock-walled windbreaks left by previous parties are the nearest thing to a built site.

bivy.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
bivy.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. Painted mountain, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a day objective with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
bivy.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
bivy.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside Glacier Peak Wilderness, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

approach_variants.name: Blanca Lake Trail to Virgin Lake, then the south-ridge climbers' path
approach_variants.notes: From the Blanca Lake trailhead at the end of the North Fork road, follow the lake trail north into the wilderness. It climbs immediately in a long series of roughly thirty switchbacks, gaining most of the day's easy elevation over the first three miles to a ridge crest — muddy, rooty and icy in wet or early-season conditions. From the ridge the trail runs on through meadows to Virgin Lake, the trail's high point before it DROPS about six hundred feet to the big lake, and a good overnight camp and the last easy reliable water before the off-trail climbing. This is where the single most common navigation error happens.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Early season adds snow on the ridge and makes the glacier variant the safer of the two.
hazards: The unsigned turnoff at Virgin Lake is the commonest error on this peak
Route-finding on the faint ridge path, which is easy to lose in brush
Loose, crumbly rock on the summit block with real exposure
Dense blueberry brush and heather on the ridge, worse late in the season
A long single push with a likely after-dark return unless camped at the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: At Virgin Lake, do not continue downhill on the main tread — that goes to the big turquoise lake below and away from the peak. Instead pick up the faint, unsigned climbers' path leaving the lake into the woods toward the ridge. It gains the peak's south ridge and follows it northeast, staying on the ridge's east side to get round minor gendarmes, levels out around fifty-three hundred feet, crosses to the west side around fifty-eight hundred, then climbs steep heather and scree working around cliff bands. The technical ground starts at a notch beside a subsidiary point, reached across a boulder field — the notch is the first place the ridge is blocked by a rock step you cannot walk around, and above it the rock turns loose and pebbly for the scramble to the summit ridge. Negative markers: if you are on obvious maintained tread descending toward a turquoise, silty lake, you took the main trail at Virgin Lake and are heading away from the peak; if you are roped up on a glacier, you are on the alternative line rather than this one.

approach_variants.name: Columbia Glacier from the Blanca Lake basin
approach_variants.notes: The alternative line onto the upper mountain, and several parties pair it with the ridge path — one for the way up, one for the way down. From Virgin Lake, take the main tread down into the basin, cross or skirt the lake's south shore on logs and boulders (poles help), then work up the boulder field and heather slopes above the north shore to the glacier toe. Stay on the glacier's east side; the west-side ice is noticeably steeper.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Best when the glacier is snow-covered enough to bridge but firm enough to travel; midday summer slush makes it slow and sliding.
hazards: Crevasses on the Columbia Glacier — low-angle but real, especially where snow is soft
Soft, sliding midday slush in summer
Wading or log-crossing the lake outlet stream
Loose, crumbly rock on the lateral moraine and at the glacier exit
Camping is banned within half a mile of the big lake, so plan the overnight around Virgin Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the rock is the glacier's exit, and it is a specific and short one: about fifty feet of ledgy, somewhat loose third-class ground taking you off the ice onto rock, after which you traverse right toward the peak's southwest side and join the ridge line higher up. The test is the exit itself — a short ledgy step, not a long climb; if you are looking at hundreds of feet of rock rising straight off the ice, you are at the wrong point on the glacier's edge. Once on rock, the pebbly, loose 'kitty litter' ground and two narrow catwalks leading toward the summit block confirm you are on the standard line. Negative marker: if you are still gaining height on ice with cliffs above you and the summit off to the side, you have gone too far up the glacier past the exit.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels down the south side toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: Rope drag and route-finding after the slab traverse make this a confusing place to arrive; the anchor is above where most parties stop
The descent is repeatedly described as windy, which throws a tossed rope off line
rappel_detail.station: About 30 m down from where the route tops out and on the skier's right, not on the summit itself. The top station is a bolted anchor - reached, from the West Face finish, by continuing about 50 ft above the top of that route's last pitch. It is worth noting where this anchor is on the way up: parties descending at dusk say knowing where the first anchors are is what makes a late descent reasonable. First of three single-rope rappels heading down toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.

rappel_detail.notes: Second single-rope rappel continuing toward the notch/gully.
hazards: This is the rappel reported as coming up about 5 ft short on a 60 m rope, finished with a short downclimb. Expect it rather than discovering it at the ends
The gully is loose and chossy, and snow-covered well into the season
rappel_detail.station: Second of the three single-rope rappels, down into the gully.

rappel_detail.notes: Third single-rope rappel reaching the notch.
hazards: The gully here is the one parties mistakenly ascend when route-finding up the chasm; on the way down it is loose and often snow-filled
Rockfall onto anyone still on the rappel above
rappel_detail.station: Third single-rope rappel, landing in the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire - often snow-covered. There is a tree at the notch that parties use as the landmark for the anchors here. A few minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing links this to the chockstone station.

rappel_detail.notes: Largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the giant chockstone (~50 ft of air) from bolts on top of the chockstone.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor on top of the chockstone
hazards: Fully free-hanging with no way to reach rock once you are on it
You arrive at this station from above by scrambling loose gully ground, which is where material gets knocked onto anyone below
rappel_detail.station: The rappel this descent is known for. Below the notch, a short scramble leads to the giant chockstone in the gully; the station is a BOLTED rap anchor on top of the chockstone - not tat, and the same bolts parties belay from on the way up when climbing the Chockstone Route. The rappel goes off the chockstone and hangs completely free for around 50 ft, and is routinely described as the longest free-hanging rappel the party has done.

rappel_detail.notes: Final short (~30 ft) rappel, or downclimb/scramble alternative, back to the base.
hazards: Loose, steep gully walking either way
rappel_detail.station: A few more minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing below the chockstone, then a last short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree to the ground. Some parties downclimb this instead of rigging it.

wa_labor_pains.rappel_count_note: These five stations are the original chockstone/notch descent down the south side, and the count assumes a single rope for the three upper rappels plus two ropes for the chockstone rappel - accounts describe it as up to five rappels depending on conditions and the number of ropes carried, and parties with two ropes throughout combine some of the upper ones. The second gully rappel comes up about 5 ft short on a 60 m. Important: many Labor Pains parties now use a different descent. A separate BOLTED rappel line was established down the West Face, running between the West Face route and Labor Pains itself, and it is that West Face line, rather than anything in this route's own gear list, that wants a 70 m rope; the list here is a 60 m. That line shares only the first anchor with the chockstone descent - from it you head down the West Face instead of into the gully - and has nothing else in common with the stations listed here. It is currently six stations on bolts and chains ending a minute from the base of the routes, with one rappel that a 60 m does not make (parties report needing to block and extend a strand, or carry a 70), and a last anchor that is genuinely hard to find, on a rib below some shrubs and skier's left as you walk down loose dirt from the fifth station. Some parties still rappel from a nearby dead tree carrying no slings, which is not the anchor. Do not blend the two lines: the station list shown is the chockstone line.

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the standard one — flat, partly wind-sheltered tent sites tucked behind the rock buttress, reached by moderate snow and loose rock bands. Reports place the platforms anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,700 ft depending on which bench and how much snow is in; the ground above the rock is more exposed and takes the full wind. There is no liquid water at any point. The approach ramps immediately below turn loose and unpleasant once they melt out, so late-season parties arrive slower than they plan.
bivy.water: none — melt snow or ice
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: a handful of existing snow platforms; can be crowded in season, and late parties dig their own

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp, and the usual way to split what is otherwise a 7-10 hour push from the car to Thumb Rock. Established sites sit in the ramp that gains the Carbon at about 7,300 ft, with more ground on the ridge crest above. Parties camp here specifically so they can cross the exposed ground under Willis Wall early and cold. Do not pitch out on the open Carbon under the wall to shorten the morning — that is the fall line for serac collapse off the summit icecap.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a few small sites in the access gully and on the ridge

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED first camp for parties not pushing straight to Thumb Rock. Composting toilet, bear boxes. Last dependable running water on the route — from here it is snow and ice, and Thumb Rock has none.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp. Liberty Ridge tops out near Liberty Cap and most parties come down the Emmons-Winthrop, so this is where a slow summit day ends rather than a forced night out high on the ice. Ranger hut and solar toilet, both potentially buried in snow — carry blue bags and pack them out. Reserve well ahead.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

bivy.name: Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
approach_variants.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
approach_variants.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts directly above the gap. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an open bench, and above the bench you cross a SNOWFIELD into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's left for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
approach_variants.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Remote with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, work into the peak's northeast basin. The route is guarded by a ridge notch, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a large vertical crack forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. If the notch you have reached can be walked through, it is not this one. Above the notch the ground eases and joins the snowfield and cirque used by the trail approach. Negative marker: if you are standing in a broad trail saddle with tread underfoot, you are at Dutch Miller Gap and on the standard line, where no such crack step exists.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
approach_variants.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford below the lake: cold and swift, and serious in snowmelt
Chief Creek ford near the head of Waptus Lake
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Very long approach far from help, with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming up from Lake Ivanhoe you climb to the gap from the east, so the check is that the trail has stopped climbing and starts to drop west toward the Middle Fork, with the peak above you on the left. The climbing starts at the first heather and rock steps above the gap and leads to an open bench, then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still beside Lake Ivanhoe or below it, you have not reached the gap yet.

approach_variants.name: Paradise and the Muir route to 8,600 ft, then east through the Cathedral Rocks notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route exits the upper Frying Pan Glacier's corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May. This is the winter and early-spring line, used precisely when the White River road to Summerland is shut and the Fryingpan approach is unavailable
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
A cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, which is why elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
A long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The decision is at 8,600 ft and it is a leaving, not an arriving. You step off the Camp Muir track while still about 1,500 ft below Camp Muir. If you reach Camp Muir you have gone too far — by a vertical quarter of a mile, on the busiest bootpack on the mountain, which is exactly why it happens.

Count what you cross: three glaciers and one rock cleaver, in this order — Paradise, Cowlitz, then a notch in Cathedral Rocks, then the Ingraham. If you have crossed the Cowlitz and walked into rock without finding a notch, you are below the notch and need to regain height. The traverse deliberately holds elevation to stay above a serac and cliff band; drifting down is the error that feels easy at the time.

The base is a ramp, and it is the only ramp: a snow or rock ramp at about 8,900 ft leading onto the south and east face. Arriving at the foot of a face with no ramp means you are round the wrong side of it.

The negative that separates this from the peak's other route: the standard line on Little Tahoma comes from the FRYINGPAN side, over Whitman Notch, from the east. This one comes from Paradise, from the southwest, and never goes near Summerland or Meany Crest. If you are looking for a notch between two glaciers with the Whitman below you, you are on the other route.

Why this route exists and when it stops working: it is the winter line, done before the Cowlitz and Ingraham become too broken to cross safely. Once those glaciers open up, the traverse is the hazard rather than the climb.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the sheepherder's traverse to the col west of Clark Mountain, then the upper Richardson Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft at the end of FR-6400, White River Trail #1507 runs almost level upstream through old growth for about four miles. The junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562 sits roughly a quarter mile past the bridge over Boulder Creek — if you have crossed the creek and seen no sign, keep walking. Turn onto #1562 and climb gently through forest to the established camp at the creek crossing near 3,700 ft; whether that is a step-across or a genuine ford depends on the year. Above camp the trail switchbacks and climbs roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about three miles into the open basin below Boulder Pass. Snow lingers in that basin well into summer, and the pass is the last of the maintained, easy-to-follow trail. Above Boulder Pass the route becomes an unmaintained sheepherder's path that sidehills east across a series of cirques, losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining height near a 7,200 ft spur. That traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach: brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or under snow. This route also carries a set of waypoints describing a different line — over the pass, down to a ford of the Napeequa near 4,700 ft, and up to a high basin at 7,000 ft under the east face. Both are real ways to this mountain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable. The Richardson has been reported thinning and breaking up in recent years, so a late-season party should expect it to be less straightforward than it used to be
hazards: Crevasses and moats on an upper Richardson Glacier that recent parties report thinning and breaking up
The sheepherder's traverse across the cirques — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in cloud or snow
A short low Class 4 step below the east ridge that can carry verglas and has no fixed anchor
Loose scree and rotten rock just below the summit block
A Thunder Creek exit that reads shorter on the map and is documented as slower, brushier and harder to follow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival at the climbing is a glacier, and the thing that gets you to it is a col that belongs to the next peak. From the 7,200 ft spur, make a rising traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy Class 2 ledges to the roughly 7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain. You are navigating to a gap beside a different summit, which is what makes it findable: Clark is the big thing on your left.

From that col, the route is one rising traverse across the Upper Richardson Glacier to Luahna's east ridge. Rope up at the col. The glacier crossing is the route; the ridge above it is a scramble west to the summit.

The critical negative marker is about which glacier you are on, and this peak's own record has already been wrong about it once: the Pilz and Butterfly Glaciers are on Luahna's north slope and belong to a separate route approached from the Napeequa side. This route uses the RICHARDSON, which lies to the south-east of the summit. If the glacier you have stepped onto is north of the peak, you are on the other mountain's business entirely.

The second negative marker is simpler: if you never touched a glacier at all, you are on the south-west slopes and south-east ridge line, which is the other route on this peak and is deliberately glacier-free. Both finish on the same summit and neither is a variation of the other.

Coming down, the one piece of technical ground is below the east ridge: a short, steep step reported as low Class 4 and sometimes verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties downclimb it; a single 20-30 m rappel off a horn or block is common practice when it is wet or icy. There is no fixed anchor — carry webbing.

Do not take the thunder creek exit on the strength of the map. Dropping south into Thunder Creek looks shorter and is reported slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown, avalanche debris and a boot path that disappears near the creek crossing. Reversing the ascent line over Boulder Pass is the reliable way out.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Basin high camp and the sheepherder's trail through four cirques
approach_variants.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft, White River Trail #1507 and then Boulder Creek Trail #1562 lead to a ford and camp around 3,700 ft, and on up into Boulder Basin. High camp is a grassy knoll overlooking the basin at about 5,800 ft. From camp the route traverses a saddle into the White River drainage and then follows the old sheepherder's path across a chain of cirques. The path is fairly well defined but the first cirque is where parties lose it and regain it repeatedly; the second, Clark Basin, is less brushy, more open and park-like with clear tread; the third, Luahna Basin, has good tread and is where parties describe camping as heaven on earth. There is a great deal of up-and-down and side-hilling on this traverse — the recorded elevation figure is far larger than for the peak's other route, which is what all that sidehill costs. This line is deliberately glacier-free, which is its whole reason to exist beside the other route on the peak.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep. A September ascent works but expect cold and the possibility of early snow on the traverse and the summit ledges
hazards: An exposed Class 3+ traverse on the north side just beneath the summit, crossed with nothing to protect it
A long sidehilling traverse across four cirques with heavy elevation loss and regain, and a path that vanishes in the first one
Loose scree and rotten rock below the summit block
Lingering snow on the traverse and ledges early in the season
Remoteness measured in a day's walk from any road, with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You find the base of this route by counting basins, and the answer is four. From the Boulder Basin camp the sheepherder's path crosses cirques in order: boulder, then Clark, then LUAHNA, and the peak's base sits above the fourth — Chalangin Basin. Nothing about the ground tells you which cirque you are in, but the character does: the first is where the path keeps disappearing, the second is open and park-like, the third has good tread. Count them.

The intermediate marker is a number on the ridge: make a rising traverse across Luahna Basin toward the roughly 7,500 ft ridge point, then follow a faint trail across scree and talus above the fourth cirque to the peak's base. Above Chalangin Basin, not in it.

The positive test at the base is the grade, and it is easier than you expect: the scramble begins on easy class 2 ledges on the south face, leading up to the right-hand skyline ridge. Class 2 ledges, south-facing, and a ridge on your right at the top of them. If your first ground is steep, or if you are on a glacier, or if the ledges lead left, you are not on it.

The confirmation comes high and it is on the wrong side of the mountain: just beneath the summit the route crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side before the final Class 3 scramble straight up. So the sequence is south-face ledges, gain the ridge, cross to the north beneath the summit, then straight up. A route that never leaves the sunny side has not reached the summit block.

The negative marker against the peak's other route: the east slopes line crosses the upper Richardson Glacier from a col west of Clark Mountain and needs glacier gear. This route touches no glacier at all. If you are roping up for crevasses, you are on the other one, and it is a different day.

A note on what is published versus what parties find: this is described as a second-class line, and most parties meet a short Class 3 or better traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. Expect it rather than treat it as evidence you are off route.

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs trailhead and the Lunch Counter
approach_variants.notes:
From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Road to the Forest Road 23 junction, bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 turn for South Climb, then FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, and FR 8040 for 8.1 miles — steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks, no RVs or trailers — to the South Climb / Cold Springs trailhead at 5,600 ft.

Permits: a Cascade Volcano Pass is required to travel above 7,000 ft in the Mount Adams Wilderness during the summer season (May 1 to September 30), and a free wilderness permit is needed for the trailhead. The wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead; the climbing pass is a single-trip pass sold only online, so buy and print it before driving up.

The trail begins on an old roadbed through burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadow, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge toward the snowfields. In early season there is often no trail at all — just a snow slope leading out of the parking lot. Above the Crescent Glacier the way is meandering snowfields to the Lunch Counter.

The Lunch Counter (roughly 9,250–9,400 ft) is the standard camp: a broad rocky bench with hand-built rock windbreaks. Water is snowmelt. This is a route where the crowd itself is a factor — it is the most-climbed line on the mountain and the bench fills on summer weekends.
approach_variants.season: Late May through September; earlier in the season the whole route is a snow climb from the parking lot
hazards: Rockfall and soft-snow postholing on the Crescent Glacier slopes in warm afternoons
Whiteout on the featureless snowfields between Crescent Glacier and the Lunch Counter
Turning around at Piker's Peak believing it is the summit
Uncontrolled glissading — the standard descent line has caused injuries
No water above the Lunch Counter; snowmelt only
Sharp switchbacks and rough surface on FR 8040, and snow blocking it early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no bergschrund and no ice step on this route, so the question 'where does the climbing start' has two answers, and the second one is the one that turns people around short of the top.

The first: the Lunch Counter is the transition. You are there when the meandering snowfields end at a broad, flat, rocky bench with rock walls built on it and the South Spur rising directly above as one continuous slope. Above the bench there is no more wandering — it is 2,400 ft of steepening snow on a bearing of roughly north-northeast.

The second, and the important one: what you top out on is NOT the summit. The rounded high point at 11,644 ft is Piker's Peak, the false summit. The test is unmistakable if you know to look for it — the ground ahead of you FLATTENS into a broad saddle and plateau, and a separate dome rises about 600 ft beyond it to the north. If the slope has stopped and the true top is still visibly above and away from you, you are on Piker's. Parties turn around here every season believing they have finished.

Negative marker on the way up: if you are scrambling on a rocky crest rather than kicking steps on snow, you have drifted onto Suksdorf Ridge. That is a legitimate alternative when the snow is soft, but when the snow is firm it is the slower choice, and in a whiteout it is the wrong handrail.

bivy.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one worth reaching — open slopes above Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, roughly a mile past the pass up the climbers' path and moraine, and preferred by parties specifically to avoid sleeping in the forest at or below the pass. Budget 7-9 hours from the road closure to here. This is the last water on the route: the snow finger to Flypaper Pass and everything on the Eel above it has none, so fill here or plan to melt. Exposed to wind, with no built shelter.
bivy.water: the tarn when melted out; often still frozen in spring, so melt snow
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays
bivy.capacity: a few tents on open ground near the tarn

bivy.name: Honeymoon Meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the last big established site on the West Fork, roughly eight trail-miles past the ranger station. Dry ground at the far end of the meadows once the snow goes. Getting here involves at least one calf- to knee-deep ford of the West Fork depending on melt, so arrive with time to deal with a high river rather than in the dark.
bivy.water: West Fork Dosewallips at camp
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays
bivy.capacity: several parties; established riverside sites

bivy.name: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative about 0.7 mile and 700 ft above Honeymoon Meadows, below Anderson Pass. Sheltered and in trees, which is its value in weather — but parties routinely walk past it without finding it under snow, so do not commit to it as your only plan on a late arrival. It is still below the pass, so it leaves the whole climbers' path and moraine for the next day.
bivy.water: creek nearby
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays
bivy.capacity: a few sites in forest

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the 4,900 ft saddle, then the boot path and cairns over Peak 5681
approach_variants.notes:
From the Austin Pass / Artist Point trailhead at the end of SR-542, follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600. It DROPS about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up past Lake Ann — 4.1 miles one way to the lake area — to a saddle at 4,900 ft northwest of the lake.

From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest. Where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms; from there follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly half a mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann.

About 10.5 miles round trip with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative gain, part of which comes from the fact that the trail loses 800 ft at the start and you pay it back at the end.

Note on the name: this is the Lake Ann below Artist Point on SR-542, not the Lake Ann near Maple Pass. One route has already been recorded with the wrong Lake Ann's trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep snow-free; winter and spring ascents are done by experienced parties with mountaineering gear on a stable snowpack
hazards: Cairns as the only navigation above 5,300 ft, in both directions
Contouring low on the return, which cliffs out above the Swift Creek basin
An 800 ft descent at the start that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
Two Lake Anns in the North Cascades, and one of them has already been given the wrong trailhead
Lingering snow on the traverse in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The 4,900 ft saddle northwest of the lake is where the route starts, and it is the last piece of maintained trail. Below it, built tread. Above it, a boot path. If you are still on graded trail heading toward the Fisher Chimneys and Shuksan, you have walked past your turn — that is the same trail, continuing.

The bearing out of the saddle is southwest, then south, along the crest. Two headings in sequence. In cloud, keep the crest under your feet.

The one place the route leaves the crest is near 5,300 ft, and it goes east. Where the ridge steepens the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms above. Contouring west here puts you on the wrong side of the ridge above the Swift Creek basin.

Cairns are the handrail above 5,300 ft, and losing them is the main route-finding hazard in poor visibility, in both directions. Note them going up.

Arrival: the scrambling ridge runs roughly half a mile west from Peak 5681 to Mount Ann's summit. Peak 5681 is not the top — if you are standing on a high point and there is more ridge running west, keep going.

And the return trap, which is worth stating because it is a cliff problem rather than a navigation one: coming back, stay high on the ridge rather than contouring low where the path is indistinct. Contouring low here cliffs out above the basin.

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail 603 and the Railroad Grade to Sandy Camp
approach_variants.notes:
Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead at about 3,400 ft, at the end of the Sulphur Creek road. Cross Sulphur Creek near the start — bridged or on logs, but a genuine ford during peak snowmelt — then climb through the meadow and forest switchbacks.

At about two and a quarter miles a SIGNED junction sends you right onto the Railroad Grade Trail 603.2. Stone steps take you up onto the crest of the lateral moraine. There are three established camp areas along the way; Sandy Camp at about 5,900 ft is the usual one for climbing, roughly four miles in with 2,600 ft of gain.

Above Morovitz Meadows there is no reliable water other than melted snow.
approach_variants.season: May-Sep
hazards: Sulphur Creek crossing during peak melt
exposed, loose moraine crest in wind
crevasses on the broad Easton, worse late season
volcanic gas and unstable ground at Sherman Crater
no water above Morovitz Meadows
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the start when the moraine crest simply runs out. The Railroad Grade tapers off just before 6,000 ft into the sandy flats and rock-walled tent platforms of Sandy Camp; that is where the trail stops being a trail and where parties rope up for the glacier.

The simplest confirmation on the way up is which side the ice is on: walking the moraine crest toward the mountain, the Easton Glacier drops away on your right the entire way. If the glacier is on your left, or if there is no glacier beside you at all, you never took the signed junction and are still on the Park Butte trail heading for the lookout.

Higher, the feature that tells you the glacier is done is Sherman Crater — steaming, sulphurous ground at the head of the ice. The Roman Wall is the steep snow rising beyond it, and the true summit is a short traverse past the top of the wall. Smelling sulphur means you are at the top of the glacier and should be turning up onto the wall, not continuing toward the crater.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
approach_variants.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
