approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Berge's north and west faces are cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go
A steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
An exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
A short fourth-class step to the true north summit, harder than the rest of the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a broad saddle on the south side at about 7,650 ft, and the way you get to it is a snow finger rather than a slope. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a snow finger and its moat, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

The saddle is where the route leaves the basin. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

The negative marker is the most important thing on this peak and it is about aspect: Berge's north and west faces are cliffy. Parties must stay on the south-west side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

The route-finding rule lower down is a descending traverse, which feels wrong and is right: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

The last obstacle has an elevation and a character: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with SLANTED SLABS and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

The summit is not one point. The true, north summit needs a short fourth-class step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy — the direct line from High Pass does not go, and this approach puts you underneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on both the Buck Creek and Napeequa approaches
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
An exposed 7,840 ft notch linking the two sides of the ridge
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, affecting the drive to Trinity
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The High Pass approach delivers you to the wrong side of the mountain on purpose, and the rule is that you must keep going around. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. The climb is on the south-west side. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

The arrival is the same place for every approach to this peak: the broad saddle on Berge's south side at about 7,650 ft, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

The approach-specific marker on the High Pass line is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

The 7,840 ft notch is the link between the two sides and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

And the same summit warning applies: the true summit is the north one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
From the Dosewallips River Road washout at roughly 550 ft, about 5 miles of road-walk or bike on the closed road, crossing Constance Creek on wooden footbridges near the start, to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,450 ft.

The trail gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — one of the steepest approaches in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutal and eases only slightly into denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps needing hands. Expect scramble-grade tread with no switchbacks and cairn-and-flagging route-finding in places. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a full pack. Water at Constance Creek partway and at the lake outlet; treat everything.

The trail skirts the lake's east shore to established campsites at the north end, in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Most parties camp there rather than going car to car. From camp, head north up scree into the canyon's lower basin, then bend east along a rib.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Residual snow in the South Chute makes it a far better climb than bare scree does
hazards: The Finger Traverse is a highly exposed, downsloping narrow ledge; footholds are marginal even with the crack in hand
Reversing it on descent goes round a blind corner and most parties find that harder than the way up
1,900 ft of loose scree in the South Chute, which sluffs rock onto parties below
The fixed pitons on the traverse are decades old — do not trust them without inspection
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics; the descent takes many parties nearly as long as the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is a tower called the Cat Ears, and the published instruction is a trigger rather than a description: begin climbing the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears are visible. Follow Avalanche Canyon north from the lake — roughly 0.6 mile — and watch east. The Cat Ears is the tower standing just left of the notch you are aiming for at the top of the chute. The moment it comes into view, turn east and start up. Starting later means more scree; starting earlier puts you on the wrong ground.

In cloud, when the Cat Ears cannot be seen, the fallback is the chute's own shape. The South Chute is a long gully that NARROWS as it climbs, gaining about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft at the notch in the south ridge. It is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake. If the gully you are in is widening rather than narrowing, or if you are still walking north up the canyon bed after well over half a mile, you have passed it and are heading for the North Chute and the Terrible Traverse instead.

Second test, and it is what confirms you were right about the chute: above the notch you cross a saddle, drop about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge. A route that only ever goes up is not this one — the deliberate loss of height above the first notch is part of the line. From there the route threads gaps and ledges marked in places by faded white paint dots. Painted dots are man-made, they do not move, and they are visible at arm's length in fog; if you are seeing them you are on the line.

The finger traverse itself is a tactile test, which is the best kind here: a downsloping ledge above a large cliff with a horizontal crack running along its top edge, which you jam your fingers into for balance because the footholds are thin. A rusty decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along it. If there is no continuous crack at hand height above the ledge you are standing on, that is not the Finger Traverse.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail entirely. From the Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles, about 1.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off, to the old campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end. Take the Constance Pass Trail up through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft, then leave the trail and go cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and up to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif.

From Crystal Pass descend south into Avalanche Canyon on an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the north side of the canyon, and continue down the canyon toward the lake until the South Chute opens on your left (east).

This is considerably longer than the lake approach and it exists because the lake trail is brutally steep, unmaintained and blowdown-choked. Most parties on it are on a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmarked cross-country travel between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass, on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass beyond transient snowmelt
Every hazard on the Finger Traverse itself, reached at the end of a longer day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Entering the canyon from Crystal Pass puts the Cat Ears test the other way up: you must descend past the North Chute before the South Chute opens. The Cat Ears tower and the formation trip reports call the Thumb both sit in this stretch of canyon, and on this side you pass them going down rather than meeting them going up.

The reliable test on this side is the chute's top, not its bottom. The South Chute tops out at a notch in the south ridge at roughly 6,600 ft, with the Cat Ears tower standing just left of that notch. Coming down the canyon from Crystal Pass you can pick your entry by which notch the gully above you leads to: the one with a tower just left of it is the South Chute. The chute that leads straight toward the Terrible Traverse without a tower beside its notch is the North Chute.

Above the chute the tests are identical to the lake approach and they are the good ones: cross the saddle, lose about 150 ft, up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge, then gaps and ledges marked with faded white paint dots, then a downsloping ledge with a continuous horizontal finger crack along its top edge and old fixed pitons in it.

Honest limit: the track fades near Crystal Pass and the drop into the canyon is unmarked. This variant is longer and navigationally harder; it is chosen for the trail it avoids, not for the ground it crosses.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail and Avalanche Canyon to the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Road-walk or bike about 5 miles up the washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at roughly 1,450 ft. The trail is unmaintained and gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — steep from the first half-mile, exposed roots and rock steps needing hands, no real switchbacks. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a pack. Camp at the lake's north end.

From camp, head up into Avalanche Canyon on scree and talus. Firm snow, when it is there, makes this whole section faster and safer than bare scree. This route takes the same South Chute as the Finger Traverse, then a second gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft. From there the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to reach the Terrible Traverse itself at about 7,435 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Steep hard snow persists longer on the Terrible Traverse than on any other crux on this mountain, which is exactly the point of it
hazards: The Terrible Traverse crosses steep firm snow directly above a large cliff — an unprotected slip is very likely fatal
Hard, icy neve is common through June and early July; afternoon softening increases slip risk later in the day
Loose rock throughout the South Chute — classic Olympic choss, and rockfall from parties above is a real hazard
Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes, called out specifically for May-June conditions
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics, hard on the way down and slick when wet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is the Cat Ears, and it is a trigger: start up the South Chute as soon as that tower comes into view. Walk north up Avalanche Canyon from the lake past the Thumb and watch east. The Cat Ears is a rock tower standing just left of the notch at the top of the South Chute; once you can see it, turn east and climb. If you are still walking up the canyon bed well after it appeared, you are heading for the North Chute instead.

In cloud, when the tower is hidden, use the chute's shape: the South Chute is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake, and it NARROWS as it climbs to the notch at about 6,600 ft.

Second test, above that notch: the line drops a little, climbs a second scree gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft, then loses height again and traverses north on ledges. Here the two crossings part company. The Finger Traverse goes up and around a corner on a ledge with a horizontal finger crack along its top; the Terrible Traverse is reached over hard-packed scree to a cairned ledge heading north, and you meet the crossing itself at about 7,435 ft. It is unmistakable when you arrive: a steep exposed snow slope directly above a large cliff, or in late season a narrow rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above it. It is called the Terrible Traverse because a slip there does not stop.

What the season changes: early to mid summer this is hard steep snow wanting an axe, crampons and, for many parties, pickets. Late season it often melts back to that rock ledge, which most parties find more secure. Neither is the wrong condition; they are different climbs.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long way in, and the one parties choose to avoid the Lake Constance trail. From the same Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 1.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Published trail mileages differ by several miles depending on where the count starts, so none is quoted. The upper stretch is open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass descend into upper Avalanche Canyon — which is where this variant differs usefully from the lake approach, because it puts you in the canyon above the lake rather than below it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow remnant below Crystal Pass is safe or gone
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and the descent into upper Avalanche Canyon is unmarked
Early-season snow remnant below Crystal Pass may want an axe and, for some parties, a rope
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt — carry it
All the Terrible Traverse hazards above, reached by a longer and more committing line
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming in from Crystal Pass you enter Avalanche Canyon from above, so you must descend past the North Chute before the South Chute opens. Dropping south into the canyon, the first couloir you meet on the Constance side is the North Chute; keep going down the canyon toward the lake.

The fixed landmarks on this stretch are the Cat Ears tower and the Thumb. The gully you want is the one whose top notch, at roughly 6,600 ft, has the Cat Ears tower standing just left of it: that is the South Chute. If you reach the lake you have gone below it.

Above the chute the test is the same as the lake approach: a short drop and a second gully to the upper notch near 7,300 ft, then the route loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft — a steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, or a narrow rock ledge in late season.

Honest limit: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and lingering snow with real route-finding. This variant trades a brutal trail for a navigation problem; in cloud it is the harder of the two.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: PLANNED first camp on the traverse, roughly three hours past Cascade Pass and the usual night one for a Formidable trip. Good sheltered ground and easy water. Mountain goats work the camp for salt — stow sweaty gear and pee well away from the sites. It is still a long day from here to the peak, so parties chasing a single summit day usually push higher.
bivy.water: lake at camp
bivy.capacity: several small parties; established sites around the tarn

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the closest ground to the north side of the peak — the col is the only non-technical crossing of the Spider-Formidable wall and it puts you directly above the Middle Cascade Glacier. Fully exposed on a notch, so expect wind and no shelter at all in weather. The slab trickle is unreliable; confirm it before counting on it, and be prepared to melt. The col itself holds steep snow into the season and parties have needed hand lines to descend the far side.
bivy.water: a trickle down nearby slabs when running; otherwise melt snow
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on small levelled spots on the col

bivy.name: Ridge benches above Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED launching camp specifically noted by parties climbing Formidable, sitting on the ridge above the lakes with a much shorter summit day than camping at the lakes themselves. The trade is water: there is none up here except what you melt or carry from below. Gaining this ridgeline out of the lakes is the most consequential bit of travel in this section of the traverse.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small; scattered flat spots on the ridge

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the south side of the col, the standard traverse night and the fallback when the col is windbound. Sheltered, easy water, and a comfortable place to sit out weather — but it is well below the peak and adds a steep, loose climb back to the ridge in the morning.
bivy.water: lakes at camp
bivy.capacity: several parties; established sites

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; stay left at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the uphill fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
hazards: Extremely shattered rotten shale with real rockfall and ankle-turn hazard the whole way up
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes, with the steepest 500-600 ft immediately off the pass
Lingering steep snow on the Constance Pass to Deception Basin traverse into July, warranting an axe
Brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the ridge crest and col on the way out
A long, committing backcountry approach far from help
Boulder Shelter sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climb is the col between Fricaba and Hal Foss, and the published test for it is the one thing about this peak that works without seeing anything: from Deception Basin, ascend eastward aiming for the lowest point in the ridge connecting Fricaba with Hal Foss. Lowest point. Not the nearest gully, not the most obvious scree fan — the lowest saddle on that connecting ridge. In cloud you can still tell which way a skyline sags by walking toward the direction the ground stops climbing soonest.

Second test, once at the col: turn away from Hal Foss and follow the ridge up to Fricaba. The North and SW ridges are the two most readily ascended and this is the SW one. The first 500 to 600 vertical feet off the pass is the STEEPEST part of the climb; after that it eases into a straightforward scree hike. So the shape of the effort is a check on the line: steep first, easy after. A route that stays uniformly moderate is not this one.

Third test, and it is which summit: Fricaba's SW peak is the true, higher top. The NE peak lies about half a mile away along the NE ridge and is noticeably lower. If you have walked half a mile of ridge from the top you reached and are now standing somewhere higher, you were on the NE peak.

What the ground feels like, so it does not read as a wrong turn: Fricaba is extremely shattered, rotten shale. Two steps up and one slide back is the normal experience, not evidence you are off route. Brief Class 2-3 scrambling appears near the ridge crest.

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the left of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A 35-40 degree snowfield below the Royal-Deception notch, wanting an axe outside late season
Shattered shale and scree on Fricaba itself
Gendarmes on the approach ridge that must be skirted rather than climbed
Long approach with the last dependable water at Royal Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same base, same test, approached across the basin rather than down into it: from Deception Basin, ascend eastward aiming for the lowest point in the ridge connecting Fricaba with Hal Foss. The extra test this side needs is the gendarmes on the way up: the usual line goes round them to the left, then up steep scree. If you are scrambling over towers rather than skirting them, you have taken the crest instead of the scree. And the same summit test: the SW peak is the true top. The NE peak, half a mile off along the NE ridge, is lower. Honest limit: the scree route above the col is considered self-explanatory, which means there is no known marker for it. It is a walk-up on rubbish rock; the navigation problem is getting to the col, not what happens above it.

approach_variants.name: Luna Col, then over the back and 2,400 ft down into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake
approach_variants.notes:
The modern approach mirrors the Luna Col line and then drops over the back: SR-20 to the Ross Dam trailhead, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, another mile to the marked cut-off, a log crossing of Big Beaver Creek just north of Access Creek, and the Access Creek bushwhack to Access Creek Basin at 4,300 ft.

From there the scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft and the steep heather traverse to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft. The whole approach is given as about 17 miles and 7,000 ft of gain from the water-taxi dock.

What is different begins at Luna Col: this route DESCENDS from it, north-northwest into Luna Cirque to Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft, then southwest to a camp on the cirque floor beneath the buttress. That descent costs 2,400 ft which has to be regained on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: 2,400 ft of descent into Luna Cirque that must be regained on the way out
The Access Creek bushwhack and the loose scree chute to Access Col
No descent down the buttress; the exit crosses the summit and the Southeast Glacier
Steep summit snow of about 300 ft, 40 degrees at the base to nearly 50 at the top, on the exit
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no realistic bailout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The 2,400 ft of descent is the test, and it is the only route on this peak that asks for it. Every other line from Luna Col goes up or across. This one goes down, and a long way down, into the cirque on the far side. If you have left Luna Col and are not losing height fast, you are on the wrong side of the ridge.

Arrival at camp: Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft is the confirmation and it is a water feature, which is what makes it findable in bad visibility. Camp is on the cirque floor beyond it, beneath the buttress. Standing at a lake at the bottom of a cirque with walls on three sides, having descended roughly 2,400 ft from a col, is unambiguous.

Arrival at the climbing: the buttress rises directly above that camp on the peak's north side. This is a 20-pitch line and the base is the toe of the buttress at the back of the cirque, not a feature part way along the wall.

What going too far looks like: continuing southwest along the cirque floor past the buttress toe brings you under the west side of the massif and the connecting ridge toward West Fury, which is a different objective and offers no way up here.

The committing fact that should shape the decision at camp: the buttress is an ascent line only. The standard exit is over the top and down the Southeast Glacier on the other side of the mountain, and a party that camped in Luna Cirque still has to regain roughly 2,400 ft to Luna Col afterwards to retrieve gear and get out.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley to La Bohn Gap and the lakes
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Necklace Valley trailhead at about 1,650 ft at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first five miles are deceptively flat, gaining only about 600 ft along the East Fork Foss River, entering the wilderness at about 1.5 miles.

Around mile 5 the trail FORDS the East Fork Foss River — there is no bridge and it runs high and cold in early-season melt, so cross in the morning at low flow. Then it turns uphill in earnest, roughly 2,400 ft over three miles of steep, root-laced switchbacks. This is the real crux of the approach for tired legs.

The grade eases at Jade Lake at about 4,600 ft and eight to nine miles, then Emerald and Opal Lakes through the swampy Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water, buggy in early summer.

From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends. Continue cross-country on an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus, up and east roughly a mile to a mile and a half and over 1,000 ft, to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes. That is the standard high camp: about 10 to 11 miles one way with over 5,000 ft of cumulative gain.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Most parties make it a two or three day trip
hazards: An unbridged ford of the East Fork Foss River around mile 5, high and cold in early-season melt
2,400 ft of steep root-laced switchbacks with a multi-day pack
Crevasse and bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant, mostly early season
Loose rock on the final class 2 scramble
Mosquitoes in the lake basins in early and mid summer
A long walk out from a remote camp if anything goes wrong
approach_variants.baseFinding:
La Bohn Gap and its lakes are the arrival, and the honest finding is that there is no longer much of a glacier to find. Measured in August 2022, the Hinman Glacier had largely disappeared, leaving stranded patches of snow and ice. So do not stand at the gap looking for a glacier front to identify. What you are looking for is the basin above the gap: mostly bare rock and permanent snowfield in most recent seasons, with crevasse and bergschrund hazard only in early season or after a big snow year.

How you know you are at La Bohn Gap: it is where the cairned climbers' path out of the head of Necklace Basin tops out at over 5,500 ft, with the La Bohn Lakes in it. If you are still in swampy lake-studded basin on maintained tread, you have not left Necklace Valley.

Which way from the gap: the summit lies east-northeast of La Bohn Gap, and this route's own recorded positions make that unambiguous — the eastward travel is roughly three times the northward. The first move out of the gap is north-northeast into the basin; after that the line swings east-northeast. A party still heading due north well above the gap is drifting off the route. The objective is the snowfield basin immediately above the lakes, which is unmistakable once you are at the gap, and easy class 2 ridge and scree ground leads from it to the summit ridge.

The final test is a distance along a ridge: from where you gain the summit ridge, the true summit at 7,492 ft is about half a mile along it. A party that tops out on the ridge and stops is half a mile short.

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes, High Pass Trail #676 over Low Pass, then the basin to the southwest spur
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065; the last two miles are rough and many parties park lower and walk the road. From the trailhead follow Winchester Mountain Trail #685 briefly; at about half a mile a signed junction splits left to the Winchester lookout and right onto High Pass Trail #676. Take the right fork.

#676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain, where steep exposed snowfields can linger into August, then goes over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is roughly two miles and an hour and a half to two hours from the trailhead. There is no reliable water past this point late season.

Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends. An unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100-200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at about 6,900 ft.

Keep the party to six or fewer and spread out. The rock here is notoriously loose even by Cascades standards.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep at best; snow lingers in the gully into August and in the avalanche chute below Winchester
hazards: Two nearly identical parallel gullies thirty feet apart, only one of which is the route
Notoriously loose and crumbly rock in the gully and on the upper ridge — helmets, small parties, spread out
An avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain holding steep snow into August
A faint boot path and cairns that disappear for long sections above the gully
No reliable water past High Pass late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two narrow parallel channels about thirty feet apart. Take the right-hand one. That is the route-finding crux of the whole climb, it is at the southwest spur around 6,900 ft, and it is the sentence to have memorised before you leave camp. Both channels are cut into the same rock face, both look plausible, and only one of them opens into broken rock and gains the south ridge cleanly.

Finding the spur itself, in order and without needing a view: leave the maintained trail at High Pass. Contour west on the climbers' path and lose 100-200 ft into the basin. Pass a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, and climb to about 6,900 ft. Losing height first is counterintuitive and correct; a party that only ever goes up from High Pass ends up on Larrabee's south arm ridge instead of in the basin under its face.

Confirm the gully by what it does: the right-hand channel NARROWS and then opens into broken rock that leads to the crest of the south ridge. A channel that stays uniform, or that cliffs out, is the other one.

Above the gully, favour the west side of the crest. There is a faint boot path and scattered cairns, and both disappear for long stretches, so this is genuine route-finding rather than following.

What the neighbouring objective looks like: from the same High Pass the col in Larrabee's south arm leads northeast to the Pleiades and the traverse under Larrabee's west flank leads to American Border Peak. Three separate objectives leave from one pass, so name yours before you set off.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the west side of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
The lower approach is shared with the peak's north-side routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft off FR-6211, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to the Leroy Creek ford at roughly 3.5 miles, then the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route steeply up into Leroy Basin around 6,100-6,200 ft, where the established camps are. That climbers' trail gains about 1,200 ft per mile — it is short and steep and hot under an overnight pack.

Where this route parts company with its neighbours is at the basin: instead of heading for the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col or the Icy Lake notch, it continues onto the peak's west side to reach the couloir system near the standard West / South Slopes ground.

The climb is short — roughly 450 m of mostly slabby Class 3 with two brief Class 4 steps — and it pairs naturally with a descent of the South Shoulder to make a loop back into Leroy Basin rather than a there-and-back.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep. This is explicitly a late-season line — it wants the snow gone and the rock dry
hazards: Loose rock among the summit-ridge towers on the traverse south
Brief exposed Class 4 moves that most parties climb without protection
Miscounting the gullies from the North Tower, which puts you on unrecorded ground on the same face
A steep unmaintained climbers' trail into Leroy Basin gaining roughly 1,200 ft per mile
A late-season route on an east-side peak, so afternoon thunderstorms and smoke are the normal conditions
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The gully is found by counting, and the thing you count from is the north tower. From the west side of the mountain the route is the second gully to the right of the north tower. Not the first, not the third. That is the entire identification, and it works in poor light because a tower is a silhouette rather than a texture.

The positive test once you are in it: the line takes the shallow right fork up slabby Class 3 rock on clean stone. Shallow, right, slabby, clean. A gully that stays a single deep cleft with no fork, or one whose rock is rubble rather than slab, is the wrong count.

The second confirmation is a sideways move: after the first slabs the route steps right into another couloir over a brief Class 4 step, then continues on sustained slabby Class 3 to the ridge crest. So the correct sequence is fork right, then move right again. If your gully runs straight to the crest with no lateral move and no short hard step, you are not on this line.

What the top of the route is not: gaining the ridge crest is not the summit. From the crest the route traverses south toward the main summit, passing around towers on the west — the right — side, with occasional brief Class 4 moves. If you top out and start going north, you are walking away from the peak.

The discriminators against this peak's other routes, all three of which start from the same basin: the North Face route crosses the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col and then DESCENDS four hundred feet on the far side before it reaches anything; the ice-fall route goes through a notch at about 7,200 ft onto the Entiat Glacier. Both of those take you away from the west side. If you have crossed a col or gone through a notch, you have left this route — it never leaves the peak's own west flank.

Carry the means to protect one move, or nothing. Most parties solo this; the Class 4 steps are brief and unprotected in practice, and there is nothing on the route that a rope helps with except those.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: This one is different. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge bivy above Observation Rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most sheltered ground on this side of the mountain: old stacked rock windbreaks sit here and parties describe it as the best bivy shelter in the area. The catch is position, not comfort — from here you still have to descend loose scree onto the North Mowich Glacier, and parties who camped here have called that descent the inefficient part of their trip. Cross-country zone; permit required.
bivy.water: none reliable — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a couple of tents on hand-built platforms

bivy.name: Edmunds/North Mowich glacier divide camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative used by parties who cross the North Mowich above Needle Rock rather than staying high on Ptarmigan Ridge. Puts you on the correct side of the glacier for the face, at the cost of more elevation to regain in the morning.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: one to two tents

bivy.name: High camp below the North Mowich headwall
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp closest to the base of the face, and the most exposed of the three. Parties who have used it wore helmets in camp because of rockfall and icefall shedding off the deteriorating headwall above; there is no fully sheltered ground up here. Worth it only when conditions are cold and you intend to start on the face within a few hours. Search around 9,200 ft first if the higher ground looks loaded — flat sites there are limited but out from under the wall.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents; flat ground is scarce and has to be dug

bivy.name: Liberty Cap saddle
bivy.notes: Emergency bivy only, on the broad saddle between Liberty Cap and the summit, used by at least one party benighted after topping out. It is more sheltered than the true summit and less wind-hammered than climbers expect, but it is an unplanned option to know about, not a camp to aim for — going there means you are spending a night above 13,000 ft with whatever you carried up the face.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: improvised, no prepared ground

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the last established campground on the White River approach. Composting toilet a short walk away and bear boxes on site. Melts out early and is the last dependable running water before the route goes onto snow and ice for good — most parties fill here rather than carry from the car.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required (reserve or self-register); designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED first-night option when the traverse from White River is split over two days; the park's own route notes list it as the standard intermediate camp before Ptarmigan high camp. Sits on the crest between the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers, which is the point — you hear serac collapse off Willis Wall all night but the crest keeps you out of the runout. Do not drop and camp on the open Carbon below the wall to save an hour.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small parties; scattered flat ground on the ridge crest, no established platforms

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

bivy.name: Puyallup Cleaver high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the usual high camp for the route, on the cleaver at roughly this height before it is left at about 8,500 ft for the glacier traverse. Mixed snow and rock, wind-exposed on a west-facing rib with nothing upwind of it. Site on the cleaver crest rather than in a runnel, and keep clear of the loose rock edges.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit also required at this elevation and on the glaciers above
bivy.capacity: a few tents on cut platforms

bivy.name: Colonnade Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the first reasonable stopping point once you leave the Wonderland Trail and start up toward the Puyallup Cleaver. It is a snow camp, so it depends entirely on coverage — in a dry year the ground here is bare and the site is much less pleasant. Parties who stop here accept a very long summit day in exchange for an easier first day off the trail.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay, obtained in person; a separate paid climbing permit is required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.capacity: snow platforms — build what you need

bivy.name: Open bivouac near 9,600 ft
bivy.notes: PLANNED but committing — used specifically to cut the summit day down, and on record as an open bivouac rather than a sheltered site. There is nothing here but what you dig. In a dry season the transition from this height onto the face is the part that turns parties around, so the higher camp only pays off if the snow is in.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.capacity: a bivy sack or two

bivy.name: Bergschrund camp in the Sunset Amphitheater
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp reached by leaving the cleaver near 8,500 ft, traversing the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers and climbing a steep snow gully to a small bergschrund with good ground beside it. The caution is the amphitheater itself: the headwall above sheds ice and rock, so this only makes sense sited where the schrund and the terrain put you out of the fall line, and it is worth reaching it early and cold rather than in afternoon sun.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp for the wall, on the northeast side of the ridge dividing the Carbon from the Winthrop. This is the camp the route is climbed from — parties leave here before midnight to reach the avalanche cones at the foot of the central rib while everything overhead is still frozen. **Do not camp out on the Carbon Glacier below the wall.** A party that pitched on the Carbon in the fall line watched a large collapse off Willis Wall run close to their tent; the ice cliff at the top of the wall is on the order of 300 ft high and it discharges straight down onto the head of the glacier. The ridge crest is the whole reason this camp exists.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small parties; flat ground has to be built by moving rocks or stomping snow

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the White River approach, which is now the practical way in — the Carbon River side lost public vehicle access when the Fairfax Bridge closed. Composting toilet and bear boxes. Last dependable running water; everything above is melt snow.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: St Elmo Pass bivy
bivy.notes: PLANNED staging bivy at the pass where parties change into glacier gear before stepping onto the Winthrop. A short rock wall gives some wind shelter and the site is out of any fall line. Useful when a late trailhead start makes the full traverse to Curtis Ridge too long.
bivy.water: none — melt snow, usually plentiful
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on a small flat bench

approach_variants.name: Shannon Ridge Trail #742 (standard)
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Baker Lake Road (FR 11) north from SR 20 near milepost 82, then FR 1152, then the 1152-014 spur to its end. The spur is rough and rutted; high clearance is the sensible minimum. An overnight in the park needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, obtained in person at Marblemount or arranged in advance with the wilderness office.

The trail opens as an old roadbed running northeast. It stays easy for roughly the first two miles, then a long-standing blowdown belt makes for tedious weaving before the tread turns into a real trail and angles left through brush onto the open crest of Shannon Ridge.

Above treeline the ridge rolls along through meadow and scattered timber to a pass at about 5,400 ft, where a major north-south ridge is joined and the Sulphide Glacier with the summit pyramid behind it comes into view for the first time. One party logged roughly four and a half hours and about 2,800 ft of gain to this point. Camps are established on the glacier's lower flats at about 6,200 ft and higher at about 6,500 ft; both have had composting toilets, but the upper one has been closed when full, so carry blue bags. There is no reliable running water above timberline late in the season.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: loose rock funnelled down the summit-pyramid gully, worst late season when the snow has melted out of it
moat between glacier and pyramid, which widens through the season
crevasses on the Sulphide as snow bridges thin after midsummer
blowdown belt on the lower trail is easy to lose in the dark
no reliable water above timberline
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts where the glacier ends against the summit pyramid, and the whole navigational problem is picking the right groove out of several parallel ones. Walk the glacier to its high point directly beneath the CENTRE of the rock pyramid — not around either shoulder. The correct line is the central gully: it is the one carrying fixed rappel anchors and old slings, because every party that summits rappels back down it, and its rock is scoured and boot-polished rather than mossy. If you are looking up a steep parallel groove with no anchors visible and clean-cut, untravelled rock, you are one gully off; traverse back toward the middle of the face.

The last few metres before rock are the giveaway that you have arrived: a short steep snow patch and then a moat where the glacier has pulled back from the pyramid. Early in the season a snow bridge spans it; by August it is an open gap you step or scramble across, and that step is the true start of the climbing. If you are still walking on flat glacier with rock only in the distance, you are short of it.

A second, separate option exists — a gully on the southwest side, reached by continuing around the western edge of the glacier until the pyramid stands squarely in front of you. It is a distinct line, not a variation of the central gully, and parties who take it still descend the central one.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the Mildred Lakes trailhead; no pass or fee is needed to park at the Putvin trailhead. Entering via Staircase/Olympic NP requires the $30 park entrance fee (7-day private-vehicle pass; $15 for a walk-in/bike individual pass) or an interagency pass, plus an $8 per person per night backcountry camping fee (booked via Recreation.gov) for Flapjack Lakes.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness regulations apply (no bikes/motorized use, max group size limits, camp 200 ft from water). Mountain goats are frequently encountered around the peak's base and Lake of the Angels basin — do not approach or feed them; give them a wide berth as they can be aggressive toward hikers seeking salt.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required for day trips on Olympic National Forest land (Mildred Lakes, Putvin Trail). Camping at Lake of the Angels, which lies inside Olympic National Park, requires an Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit. If approaching via Flapjack Lakes inside Olympic National Park, an overnight wilderness camping permit is required, reservable on Recreation.gov for the Flapjack Lakes zone (bookable mid-April, camping dates mid-June through mid-October); contact the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.
access.closures: UPDATED (as of July 8, 2026): the Mildred Lakes Trail (#822) and Mildred Lakes Trailhead on FS-25 — along with the Mt. Rose Trail/Trailhead, Dry Creek East Trailhead, and the Staircase developed area (campground, ranger station, Rapids Loop Trail) — REOPENED on July 8, 2026 per a joint Olympic National Forest/Olympic National Park press release, ending the closure tied to the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire. Still closed pending hazard-tree removal and infrastructure repair: wilderness trails beyond the developed Staircase area, including the North Fork Skokomish River Trail (from the Staircase Rapids Loop to Home Sweet Home) and the Flapjack Lakes Trail, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, plus FS-2451 and the Copper Creek Trail (Olympic National Forest alert updated July 8, 2026). The Putvin Trail/Lake of the Angels approach, on a different drainage further north off Hamma Hamma River Road, was never part of this closure and remains the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. Always check the Olympic National Forest alerts page and NPS Olympic fire-conditions page before a trip, as backcountry trail status keeps changing as repair work continues through summer 2026.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District) for the Mildred Lakes and Putvin trailheads; Olympic National Park (Wilderness Information Center) for the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish/Flapjack Lakes side.
access.land_manager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: None for day use; NPS wilderness permit for overnight camping.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit
overnight_permit.where: Get it in advance on Recreation.gov, by phone, or in person at a park Wilderness Information Center.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
approach_variants.notes: This is the standard approach and the route's waypoint list describes a different one. Published and trip-report accounts are consistent that Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stand at Lake of the Angels and the cirque itself tells you which way to go: Mount Stone is on your right, another peak is on your left, and Mount Skokomish is straight ahead. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

The turn is around the right-hand side of the lake, on a way trail heading west to the ridge. Then take a broad gully southwest and up toward the saddle just north of point 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud, which is why it is quoted here rather than a description of the terrain.

Second test, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours south and southwest across scree, grass and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn. The tarn is the confirmation. Turn right and start climbing when you are above the large tarn — that is the published trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

Third test, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around left to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has three summit horns and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

Explicit warning from a trip report, and it is directional: contouring too far right (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut west over the ridge instead.

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.notes: Recorded because the route's own waypoints describe this approach, not because it is the standard one. It is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford Huckleberry Creek at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot root and rock ladders, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base on this side is the open basin and saddle beneath the south peak at about 5,500 ft, and the test for it is underfoot: the footing turns to loose, rotten rock from there up. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. The test for the approach itself is the root ladder, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then DESCENDS off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. Honest limit, and it is the reason this variant is second: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. Published and trip-report accounts put the standard route on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer left to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues west, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
The steep steps turning to bare ice or dry-tooling ground later in the season
Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp
An unmarked, often snow-covered off-trail turn out of the Mountaineer Creek valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: The north ridge rock rib decides it, and the side it is on is the answer. From the basin you are looking at four things in a row: the Sherpa Glacier, the Ice Cliff Glacier, the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, and beyond it the Stuart Glacier. You want to be past the rib. So: if the North Ridge rib is on your left (east) you are on the Stuart Glacier and correct. If it is still on your right you have not gone far enough west and are on the Ice Cliff side. That is the same test the Ice Cliff Glacier route uses, read in the opposite direction, and it is the reliable one in cloud because it does not depend on seeing the summit. Second test — what the couloir leads to. This couloir does not go to the summit. It goes to a notch in the west ridge, which is on the far side of the mountain from where you camped. If the line you are looking up appears to head for the top of the peak, you are looking at the wrong feature. Third, the shape. Entry is at about 7,800 ft and the couloir NARROWS above you before it widens again — moderate snow, then a short steep step, then a second shorter one, then an open snowfield. A line that is uniformly wide with no steps is not this one. And the negative test: no hanging ice cliff or serac band should be above you anywhere. If there is one, you are back on the Ice Cliff Glacier, on the wrong side of the rib.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead, Trail #611 and the east gully to the saddle
approach_variants.notes: Park at the end of the forest road above Baker Lake and follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail into the woods. At about a mile, stay right or straight where the Anderson Butte Trail climbs left toward the old lookout site. Around 4,700 ft a second junction splits: the right fork drops to lower Anderson Lake, the left fork climbs a short way to a small saddle at the wilderness boundary before dropping to the Watson Lakes. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and are the last reliable water, since nothing higher on the mountain runs dependably — treat before filling. The maintained trail ends there; from the basin the route becomes an open, cairned climbers' line up talus and, well into summer, snow. Established bivy sites on open slopes around 5,400 ft shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding across the unmarked basin and ridge in flat light is the main difficulty of the approach, since there is no tread to follow.
approach_variants.season: July through September is most reliable, though snow often lingers in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into early July. Many parties prefer August for drier ground and fewer mosquitoes. An axe is worth carrying even in mid-summer.
hazards: a moat and unstable snow bridge that develop in the west-side gully late season
lingering snow in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into July
an airy summit ridge with drop-offs on both sides near the top
off-trail route-finding through talus and heather above the lakes, with nothing marked
loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle on the descent
heavy mosquito pressure at the lakes through summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two gullies lead to the saddle and only the eastern one is safe, and the summit gully is the one choked with trees. Getting to the ridge first: from the basin, take the WIDEST gully east of the peak up to the saddle at about 5,900 ft. The western gully looks like an alternative and is not — it develops a large moat and an unstable snow bridge late in the season and parties have been forced to reroute out of it. From the saddle, head west and scramble the ridge on its south side, over easy heather and treed slopes, into the basin below the true summit; cross that basin, crossing one more small snowfield, to a heather-and-dirt gully immediately on the south side of the summit block. That gully has an unmistakable signature: partway up it squeezes tight through a clump of trees, tight enough that packs have to come off and be passed through by hand. If the gully you are in is clean rock with nothing growing in it, it is not this one. Above the squeeze, the final block is a short scramble on rock that takes hands, and then a narrow ridge of around thirty feet with real drop on both sides — a hand line is commonly carried for that section and is the sensible call in either direction.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. From the lower, eastern end walk about fifty yards downhill to the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the base of the Lower Wall.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
Roofs overhead at the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The two trails out of this one pullout go to different halves of the crag, and taking the western one puts you on Logger's Ledge at Upper Castle — a full wall above where this route starts.

Mr. Clean is on the Lower Wall along with Brass Balls and the west-to-east run of The Fault, Catapult, The Vertebrae and The Bone. The Fault is the fixed reference: the short trail from the right of the parking area leads straight to it.

The Lower Wall announces itself by the many roofs overhead and by Logger's Ledge running above you. Older lines here are on gear; the NEWER routes on the right side of the wall carry more bolts, so an unexpectedly bolted line means you have drifted east of where you meant to be.

approach_variants.name: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft. Three long gravel drives reach it — from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek road, which is the roughest and where high clearance is worth having; from the Methow Valley; or the longer South Fork line over Baldy Pass, which is the gentlest on a low car. All are an hour or more of gravel. A trailhead further along the ridge system also serves the area.

From the campground, trail #373 runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft in roughly forty-five minutes of easy walking. That pass is the hinge of the whole approach.

The roads are snowbound most of the year and typically open around late June, which is awkward here: this route wants snow and the road wants none. The overlap is narrow and it is the reason this line gets climbed so rarely.
approach_variants.season: June into early July while the snow is still continuous; by mid-summer it degrades to scree and dirt
hazards: Avalanche and wet-snow release in the only window when the route is in condition
The narrow upper section is the crux and steepens to around fifty-five degrees
Road access and route condition barely overlap; too early and you cannot drive in, too late and the snow is gone
The unmaintained descent trail above the lower lake is faint and easy to lose
Long gravel drives from every direction and no quick way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Honeymoon Pass, leave the trail and traverse south along the open grassy east slope below the ridge crest into the small cirque at the foot of the north face, at roughly 7,360 ft. The face rises about six hundred and fifty feet above that cirque and it is split into two halves by a rock tower.

The face has two kinds of line and they are on opposite sides. Snow gullies on the left, a rock tower and its ridge on the right. This route is on the left. If you are standing under a tower of rock with an arete running up to it, you have walked too far right and you are under the two rock routes.

Among the gullies on the left, take the longest, most continuous and most direct one — the chute that runs unbroken from the cirque floor to the summit ridge without stepping out onto rock. The others are shorter and more broken. Sighting up the line from the cirque floor is the test: you should be able to follow one connected ribbon of snow all the way to the skyline.

Condition is part of the identification here, not a separate question. The gully averages about forty degrees with steeper sections to fifty-five, and the crux is where it NARROWS high up. If the narrow section is bare scree and dirt rather than snow, the route is out — this line does not work as a rock climb, and by late summer that is its normal state.

Negative marker on the descent, which is not a reversal: from the top of the couloir on the summit ridge, walk off by the north-west ridge, then drop to the old unmaintained trail above the smaller lake to the north-east and follow it back down to trail #373 near Honeymoon Pass. Downclimbing the couloir in afternoon conditions is the mistake this descent exists to avoid.

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek washout, Nooksack Cirque, Price Lake moraine and the ridge to the 5,900 ft slab bivy
approach_variants.notes: From the Mount Baker Highway, turn left onto Nooksack River Road (FS-32) immediately before the Nooksack River bridge, about 13 miles past Glacier. Stay left at 0.5 miles, right at 1.4 miles, and park at the washout at 2.3 miles from the highway, by Ruth Creek at about 2,156 ft. Walk the abandoned road beyond the washout for two miles to the original Nooksack Cirque trailhead at 2,550 ft. Ford the Nooksack. There is a recorded log crossing near N48.87097 W121.61267 — new logs get swept away every year, so treat the coordinate as where to start looking rather than as a bridge. Go up the forested mountainside east of the creek, starting on the west bank of Price Creek until a good log turns up. Continue to the moraine above Price Lake at 3,911 ft, then follow the ridgeline between the Price and East Nooksack Glaciers up to a rock slab bivouac around 5,900 ft. From the bivy, get onto the glacier, traverse climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, then drop down and work onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. This route belongs to Nooksack Tower and not to Mount Shuksan — it was merged from a duplicate Shuksan entry, and the Price Glacier route on Shuksan is a different climb sharing much of the same ground.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier the river is high and the couloir is safer; later the river drops but the couloir bakes and sheds rock
hazards: Fording the Nooksack on logs that are swept away and replaced yearly
Rockfall down the couloir, recorded on the first ascent and in every account since
A hollow bergschrund that has forced parties to swing wide left
A descent of roughly ten 60 m rappels off gear you build yourself — fixed anchors here should not be trusted
Parties routinely still on the couloir or the lower approach after dark; one team took 21 hours from camp back to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The bergschrund at roughly 6,500 ft is the base, and the couloir above it is the only one. Beckey and Schmidtke's own account of the first ascent puts them at the bergschrund at the foot of the final north face at 6,500 ft, with 800 ft of 50-degree ice couloir above. That is the arrival: a schrund, then a single steep couloir that guards the Tower.

The ridge between the two glaciers is the handrail. From the Price Lake moraine you climb a rib with the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. In cloud you do not need the Tower: keep a glacier on each side of you and go up. If you only have ice on one side, you have come off the rib.

The saddle is the hinge, and it is counterintuitive.
