From the bivy the traverse is climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, and then you drop down onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. Losing height here feels wrong and is correct. A party that refuses to descend off the saddle stays high on the wrong side and never reaches the couloir.

Confirm at the schrund: the couloir starts around 50 degrees and steepens to about 60 at the top, with a single 70-degree step where it hits rock. If your line eases off rather than steepens, it is not the couloir. Parties have found the schrund hollow and swung wide left to avoid it entirely — that is a known variation, not a sign you are lost.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Price Glacier past the Tower's couloir puts you on the Price Glacier route on SHUKSAN, which is a different mountain's climb reached from the same basin. Nooksack Tower is the freestanding tower below and north of Shuksan's summit; if the ground above your couloir keeps going for thousands of feet rather than ending on a tower in about 1,200 ft of fourth class, you are on Shuksan.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just under a mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, trend left of the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, and work up into the gully that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in the Concord-Lexington gully
lingering firm snow or névé in the upper gully into early summer — axe or traction useful
the descent uses slung horns rather than fixed anchors, so carry spare webbing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route does not start from the high point of the col. From the crest, move slightly west and drop a couple of feet: the first pitch begins at an obvious slanting, right-leaning crack in the Lexington side of the notch, and the 5.7 crux is the very first thing you climb — awkward moves straight off the ground. Follow the leaning crack for about 15 to 20 feet and it eases into stemming up a chimney at around 5.6. If your first moves are easy you are probably on the Concord wall opposite, which is the South Face of Concord and starts by walking gravelly ledges rather than pulling on a crack. A hard start on a right-leaning crack, just below and west of the col, is the confirmation.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through late Jun
hazards: firm snow in the gully below the col
moat where snow meets the Lexington wall
SR-20 closed in winter — no vehicle access until reopening
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow in the col the slanting crack that starts the route can be partly buried, and the couple of feet of drop west from the high point may instead be a step down into a moat. The feature to hold onto is that the start is on the LEXINGTON side, slightly west of and just below the crest, at a right-leaning crack, and the hardest climbing of the first pitch is immediately off the deck. If snow has filled the crack's base, expect to start higher up it than the summer start and to be dealing with wet rock for the first body length.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier's true-right margin to the lowest point of the buttress
approach_variants.notes:
As for the Colchuck Glacier route: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed fork, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,200 ft, and the last reliable water on the route.

Follow the east-shore boot path to the inlet at the south end, then climb talus and snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Instead of continuing toward the col, angle up and across the glacier's true-right margin toward the peak's northeast side.

Cross the moat where snow meets rock — a snow bridge or a wedged block in a good year, and the technical crux of the approach in a lean one. Parties do rope for this.

Given fourteen-plus pitches and a multi-stage approach, most parties either start well before dawn from the car or camp at Colchuck Lake and climb from there. There is no water above the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the rock; the moat crossing is easiest early and hardest in a lean year late
hazards: A moat crossing that can be the technical crux of the day in a lean snow year
Two established starts that do not converge until around pitch five
Inconsistent rock — clean crack pitches interspersed with loose, mossy and lichened ground
Loose debris on the long rising ledge traverse, onto anyone below
No water above Colchuck Lake
A long walk-off down the Colchuck Glacier after a fourteen-pitch day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The buttress is the rock just south of the couloir, and the couloir is the thing you look for first. It is easier to identify a deep slot in a face than a rib on it, so use the Northeast Couloir as your marker and then step south onto the rock beside it. If you are in a narrow snow slot, you are one feature too far north.

Arrival is the lowest point of the rock. The commonly climbed start gains the buttress at its lowest point and heads for wide, broken cracks at about 5.8. Standing at the right place there is nothing lower to climb — the rock runs down into the glacier and the moat, and you had to cross that moat to reach it.

Two starts exist, and mixing them is the routine error here. There is the more travelled version described above and an older, separate start; they do not meet until around the fifth pitch. So a party that steps onto rock wherever the moat happened to be crossable can find itself on neither, on unfamiliar ground, with no way to tell. Cross the moat where it puts you at the LOWEST rock, not where it is most convenient.

Confirmation in the first two pitches: wide, broken cracks on generally solid rock leading to the crest below a large headwall, then a downclimb of about fifteen feet off the crest before ramps take you up and right. A start with no downclimb in the first few pitches is not this line.

And the bail-out warning: this route has a real reputation for parties retreating because they cannot find the crux dihedral higher up. If the base was ambiguous, the rest of the day will be worse.

approach_variants.name: Straight off the road end: the C-J couloir to the hanging glacier, then the leftmost rib
approach_variants.notes:
This is one of the shortest approaches in the range and one of the least forgiving. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road near 3,600 ft, walk a short way back down the road, descend a dirt embankment, ford or cross the infant Cascade River, and cross the terminal moraine and snowfield. Serious ground starts around 3,500 ft — you are on the route within an hour of the car.

Climb PARTWAY up the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir to the hanging glacier on the right, then take the leftmost rib to the summit. Twelve pitches, about 4,000 ft.

The descent is a separate expedition: the East Ridge's loose 3rd and 4th class gendarme ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, then either the couloir or 'Doug's Direct' — beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehilling steep heather, across Mixup Peak's north ridge and down to the Cache Glacier. Parties have taken four and a half to nine hours from the col.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, once the road is open and the lower couloir approach holds consolidated snow
hazards: Hanging glaciers above the route — the Sill Glacier among them — that release ice and rock; parties describe rocks and ice bouncing for three or four seconds at a time
The mountain's standing reputation for rockfall, with loose rock reported across trip reports and a documented near-miss on a 2020 descent
Steep 45-60 degree snow on approach and descent with real fall consequence — one party found the heather descent the most dangerous part of the trip
A Cascade River ford at the very start, which rises through the day
A routefinding-intensive descent with suspect rappel anchors, and a history of parties returning a day or two late
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test for this route is whether you are touching vegetation, and it is the cleanest discriminator on the whole face. This side of Johannesburg carries at least five named lines within a few hundred metres of each other, and most of them start with hundreds of feet of vertical bushwhacking — alder, turf, tree roots, tunnelling through near-vertical pines. This route does not. Its own published description ends with the words no bush climbing. If you are pulling on trees or heather to make upward progress, you are on the northeast rib or the northeast buttress, not on this.

So the sequence is: stay in the couloir. Do not break out onto rock low down. Climb the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir until a hanging glacier appears on your right — that glacier is the landmark, and it is what you leave the couloir for. The Northeast Rib lines leave the couloir far lower, before it narrows.

From the hanging glacier, take the leftmost rib. That is the whole route-finding instruction and the word that matters is leftmost. Several rib features present themselves at that shelf; the correct one is the far left of them.

Orient yourself on the face as a whole before you start, because it is crowded: running west to east across it the order is the Northeast Rib lines, then a route in a vertical cleft with a waterfall, then the Northeast Buttress. The Cascade-Johannesburg couloir is the broad snow line that separates Johannesburg from Cascade Peak, and this route uses it as a stairway rather than climbing it to the col.

And know what the couloir itself is: it is the original 1938 line and the most popular one, finishing at the col rather than on any rib. If you are still in the snow at the top, you never left for the rib.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the West Face meadows
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft; Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread gives out at a washout below the West Face basin, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in.

Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft and is usually flagged pink — then climb steeply through forest to about 4,900 ft, cross talus and a meadow bench, and reach the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Water here or at the streams just below.

From the saddle stay in the meadows below the broad West Face. Do not continue southeast toward the glacier toe.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Brushy, blowdown-choked washout where the maintained trail ends
Route-finding through the forest band above the washout
Loose rock in the meadow-to-face transition
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Northwest Buttress is reached on foot with no glacier travel at all, and that is the test: if you are putting crampons on, you have walked past it onto the standard Corkscrew line. From the meadows, the route starts at the lowest and left-most point of the face, on a corner of noticeably DARKER rock than the wall either side of it. Rock you can walk up to dry-shod, with grass and meadow underfoot rather than ice, is the correct base.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: This one is different. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

approach_variants.name: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Eldorado approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount, backtrack a short way downstream to a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft with scattered camps near 6,100 ft. Most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — roughly 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft, five to six hours car to camp.

From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through or near the TEPEH TOWERS saddle, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season.

Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, trending northwest to its top. This is the easiest established route on the peak and is commonly used as the descent for the harder ones.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, depending on glacier and moat conditions
hazards: Crevasses on the McAllister Glacier, variable by year and generally avoidable
A large moat where the route gains the ridge, which deteriorates significantly by late summer
Aging and degraded rappel webbing left by past parties — one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here
Fractured rock with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is a small col at the toe of the ridge, at the top of the McALLISTER glacier's 30-degree apron, and the thing directly above it is a line of gendarmes on the crest. Gendarmes on the skyline above a small col at the top of the apron is the confirmation.

Cross the moat at the col, not at the snow gully. There is an alternative snow gully nearby that parties sometimes use to gain the ridge, and it is guarded by a large moat that usually still needs a short rappel to bypass. The route's own start is easy fifth-class rock straight off the small col at the toe. If you are eyeing a snow gully with a big gap at its head, you are looking at the alternative, not the route.

The length test is decisive on this peak because the four routes are wildly different lengths: this one is three pitches, each well under 25 m. If you are running full rope lengths, or if you are still climbing after three, you are on the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from the other side) or the East Ridge (a long day off a different col).

A fixed-gear confirmation, and a warning with it: the crest carries a lot of old fixed slings on rock horns left by earlier parties, and higher up a PITON marks a slabby section leading to a V-slot gully. Plenty of tat on horns is a sign you are on the trade line — but it is aging tat, an anchor block has failed here before, and it should be backed up rather than trusted.

And know which side of the needle you are on: this route is reached by climbing the McAllister's apron northwest. The Southwest Buttress lines are reached by continuing to the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass and dropping about 700 vertical ft to a snow gully below it. The East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle. Three different cols; check which one you crossed.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the northwest ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 6,400 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill on Old Snowy's west flank.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The turn off the PCT is unmarked, and it is the only thing on this route you can get wrong.

The test that works in fog is about motion, not landmarks: the PCT here is SIDEHILLING — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is the first thing that turns uphill and stops contouring, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

The negative is equally mechanical: if the PCT starts descending on the far side of the mountain, you have walked past the turn. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

Distance cross-check: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

Second marker, and it sits before the turn rather than after it: a persistent SNOWFIELD on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A soft confirmation at the saddle, worth knowing because it is visible from a distance: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

Base of the scramble: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

And a negative that is about visibility rather than ground: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.

approach_variants.name: Sloan Creek Road, the lookout trail, and the southwest ridge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the campground and trailhead at the end of the road up the North Fork Sauk. The signed trail there is the valley trail, but this route splits off almost immediately: look for the signed lookout trail branching left about a hundred yards in. It is low-key enough to walk straight past — if you have been on the main trail more than a couple of minutes you have missed it. The lookout trail switchbacks steadily through old growth for about a mile, gaining roughly seven hundred to a thousand feet, and ends on a flat bench where the fire lookout once stood, with views into the basin below. That is the last easy-to-follow section of the day and where most hikers turn around. Above it the path keeps climbing steeply and a cliff band appears within a few hundred vertical feet. Beyond the cliff band, an intermittent boot track marked with old pink flagging follows the crest and southwest side of the ridge through open meadows. There is no reliable water past the lower creek crossings, and the upper half is dry, south-facing and sun-exposed, so carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. Snow can linger on the ledges and the ridge boot path into July in heavy-snow years, hiding the flagging and icing the ledges. The scramble is far safer and easier to navigate dry.
hazards: an exposed ledge scramble of about seventy vertical feet just above the end of the maintained trail — loose dirt on rock, slick when wet, and harder facing outward on descent
a faint, unmaintained boot path above the ledges marked only by intermittent pink flagging, easy to lose in fog
loose scree and talus on the upper southwest ridge and summit slopes
lingering snow that can hide the flagged path into July
an open, exposed ridge with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
no reliable water above the lower creek crossings
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scramble starts where the maintained tread dies at the old lookout bench, and the ledges switchback rather than go straight. Walk the lookout trail to the flat bench around 2,800 ft where the fire lookout once stood; that bench is the reference point and the maintained tread effectively ends there. Keep climbing steeply and a cliff band appears within a few hundred vertical feet. The route takes about seventy vertical feet through it on a series of ledges, and the shape of the line is the test: it SWITCHBACKS up the ledges rather than climbing the rock directly. The ledges themselves are steep rock covered in dirt and moss rather than clean stone, so they feel insecure, and that is normal here. If you are forcing a direct line up clean rock, you are off the route. Above the band, the confirmation is pink ribbon flagging on an intermittent boot track along the crest and southwest side of the ridge. Two more checkpoints higher: the visible path effectively ends around 5,800 ft at an overlook above the small tarn in the basin, and there is a last band of stunted trees near 6,700 ft, also flagged, above which there is no ground cover at all. Note where you leave the timber, because that spot is not obvious from above on the way down. The summit above is a broad massif of red-stained rock and loose scree.

bivy.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
bivy.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. Painted mountain, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a day objective with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
bivy.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
bivy.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside Glacier Peak Wilderness, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is a saddle inside the buttress, at about 6,100 ft, and you get there by losing height first. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 ft descending traverse east across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

So the test in cloud is the shape of the ground, not the view: you go down and east for a thousand feet, then up a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

What going too far looks like: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

Confirm on the climb: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
approach_variants.notes: The line the recorded distance reflects. From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
In this drainage the navigation rule is about height, not direction, and it is the one thing that makes the day work. The creek must be forded in places, and fords get harder the lower and farther downstream you are. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

Arrival, which is unambiguous even with no visibility: above the brush line the drainage OPENS into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

From there the base test is the same one the northern approach uses: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A real risk peculiar to this approach, recorded because it has happened: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

bivy.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
Cleaver crest col
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the best ground on the route: a broad saddle on the cleaver crest that is generally out of the rockfall lines, which very little else on this cleaver can claim. No water. Above it the crest includes a knife-edge that has to be scrambled once the snow melts off it, so leaving from here in the dark is easier early season when it is still snow-covered. Some parties instead stop around 10,200 ft, which is also comfortable but leaves more of the crest for summit day.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents; platforms stomped or dug into snow

bivy.name: Devil's Dream camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED low camp about five miles in on the Wonderland Trail, in trees below Indian Henry's. Useful mainly as a bail-out or a late-start first night — it is well below the climbing and adds a lot of gain to day two. Reliable water is the reason to stop here.
bivy.water: reliable creek water at camp
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated trailside camp
bivy.capacity: designated trailside sites, small

bivy.name: Dug platform on the lower-mid cleaver
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative for parties who run out of daylight low on the cleaver. Reports describe digging in here specifically because the spot felt protected from the rockfall lines running down either side — the lower cleaver is loose choss with real exposure to anything a party above knocks down, so on this route the shelter of the platform is the point rather than the view.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: one tent on a dug platform

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and the standard first night on the traverse — the first place with water and flat ground after Cache Col. Sites sit on the lip of a steep slope that drops thousands of feet toward the valley, so pitch back from the edge in wind. The col above holds snow well into July and there is no water at the col itself, so parties crossing late in the day carry water up or drop to this lake. Goats work the camp for salt; keep gear and urine spots away from tents. The national park boundary runs at Cache Col just above; camps from here south are commonly described as lying in the wilderness outside the park where no camping permit is required, but confirm the zone with the ranger station when you pick up your trailhead permit.
bivy.water: the lake, and snowmelt runnels feeding it
bivy.capacity: several tents

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the usual second night, in heather meadow among granite boulders below the Le Conte Glacier. It is a low point on the traverse and melts out later than its elevation suggests — a party in late June found nothing bare and pitched on snow with running water alongside. Sheltered relative to the passes on either side, but the basin is a cold sink. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: the lakes; flowing water available even under snow cover
bivy.capacity: several tents

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the last true alpine camp and the one most parties would not skip, looking straight across at the icefalls of Dome and Sinister. Dry dirt bivy platforms are usable by late June, earlier than the lower camps. It is an open basin with nothing to hide behind: one party sat out roughly twelve hours of rain and wind in tents here, so anchor well and pick a site with a boulder on the windward side. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: the lakes
bivy.capacity: at least three good sites; more on snow

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows / Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the last night for parties exiting south to Downey Creek, in heather meadow below Itswoot Ridge. Melts out late — a late-June party found the lake still largely frozen, the basin barely opened up, and a marginal perch near 6,200 ft below the basin that they would not recommend sleeping on until more snow had gone. Popular enough that solitude is not the reason to stop here; proximity to the Bachelor Creek descent is. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: Cub Lake outlet and meadow streams
bivy.capacity: many parties; the meadows absorb a dozen or more groups on a holiday weekend

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes / South Cascade Glacier Col

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib, then the ledge system below the col
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain rather than for the spires, and the climbers' path itself is unmarked.

Go down the talus and into the forest, cross Early Winters Creek on a log, and climb the steep timbered rib on the left, the north side, of the creek draining the col. About two hours brings you to the basin bench at roughly 6,500 ft, where there is a spring — the last reliable water.

From the bench another three-quarters of an hour or so gains the col at about 7,720 ft. Unlike its neighbour on the same pinnacle, this route wants you high, so keep going up.

The pullout is where most parties sleep. It is undeveloped and the highway is audible all night.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access ends with the highway closure
hazards: A very loose slope is crossed to gain the approach ledge, above the col trail
The route starts at the far right end of the ledge, not where you step onto it
Precariously stacked blocks and flakes on the scramble toward the neighbouring spire
Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route is reached from high, not from low, and that single sentence separates it from the other line on this pinnacle.

There are two ways onto its ledge, described from opposite directions and they meet in the same place. Either cut right off the col trail before topping out, crossing a very loose slope to gain the left end of an obvious ledge system; or go all the way to the col and descend about three hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank to the same ledge. Both are quick.

Then walk the ledge rightward to its far end. This is the step people skip. The ledge is third class and it goes further than you expect; the route does not start where you step onto it. Keep going until the ledge runs out.

At the far right end of the ledge, a steep clean corner rises straight off it. That corner is the route. It is a big obvious corner system on the right side of the pinnacle's main face, and the climbing in it is continuous, clean and steep — the physical test is that the rock quality is conspicuously better than the loose slope you crossed to get there.

Confirm on the climb. Pitch one is moderate with a chimney-behind-a-block move. Pitch two is the standout: a steep continuous corner to a triangular roof, passed on finger locks. Pitch three is the hardest, off a detached flake into steep flaring finger and hand jams on the left wall. Pitch four is corner climbing into an offwidth section. A triangular roof on the second pitch and a detached flake on the third are the two features that settle it.

Negative marker: if you left the trail down at the bench around 6,600 ft, contoured right past a spring in a dry sandy gully, and found a CHOCKSTONE at the toe of a ridge, you are at the other route on this pinnacle — several number grades easier and a different day. A chockstone at a ridge toe is not this climb; a corner at the far right end of a ledge is.

Second negative marker: the neighbouring spire's routes start from the col itself and are the usual link-up partner. Standing at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are here; you still have to lose height.

At the top, either scramble third-class ground north-east toward the neighbouring spire's north face to continue a link-up, downclimbing over precariously stacked blocks and flakes, or make two thirty-metre rappels down the gully back to the col.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road; the crag is a few hundred feet above the houses just downstream of the lot.

Walk back along the road about 0.1 mile to a driveway signed to the effect that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk. Follow it to a retaining wall, then take the trail rising to the right toward the crags; a sign marking the boundary onto public land appears shortly after leaving the driveway. The path continues up past smaller outcrops — about 30 minutes in total.

The lower ground is private. Start near the parking lot and traverse above the residences rather than cutting through them.
approach_variants.season: Early season — south-facing with little shade and no relief in high summer
hazards: Private land on the lower approach
South-facing, little shade, hot
A thin crux crack right off the deck on pitch one
Ledge tiers that make it easy to mistake which level you are on
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Regular Route takes the prominent DIHEDRALS running up the middle of the biggest rock face on the crag, aiming straight at a large lone tree. Those are three independent things you can check from below: biggest face, obvious corner system, single conspicuous tree at the top of the line.

The first-pitch test is the thin crack right at the start — that is the crux of the whole route, and it is protected by BOLTS above the thin section. So a hard, thin opening followed by bolts confirms it; if your first pitch is easy or the corners are clean and moderate from the ground, you are on one of the upper tiers or a neighbouring route.

Everything above the first pitch is easier: clean, enjoyable dihedrals on gear from about half an inch to two inches, with small nuts and TCUs on the last pitch.

If you are at the left edge of the rock rather than in the middle of the big face, you are at Careno Corners and Bale/Kramar.

There is an obvious walk-off after pitch three, though the route carries on for a fourth.

approach_variants.name: Tieton Road spring and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes: From the highway west of Naches, carry on past the Rimrock Lake dam and turn south onto the reservoir road. Drive a couple of miles down it and park in one of the pullouts a short way past a spring marked by a split-rail fence — the fence is the landmark, not a sign or a sign-board. Walk back to the spring and pick up the steep climbers' trail that leaves from the right-hand side of it. The trail is short but steep and gains the base directly. Rattlesnakes are documented on both the approach and at the cliff base, so watch where you put hands and feet in the scrub.
approach_variants.season: May to October — the area melts out early and stays climbable late, but it bakes in midsummer.
hazards: Loose material sits on the slopes above the cliff and comes down — helmets on from the base
Rattlesnakes documented on the approach trail and at the cliff base
A past rockfall event closed part of this area for over a month; rockfall exposure here is recurring rather than theoretical
Steep, loose climbers' trail with poor footing when dry and dusty
Loose rock increases with height on this route, and a hanging boulder field sits above the top pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding: The trail itself is the marker for this route: it climbs from the spring and TERMINATES at the base of this climb. Where the boot track stops gaining height and you are standing under rock with no path continuing upward, you are there. Confirm by looking up — the opening pitches run up a face directly below a prominent roof, and the first four or five belay stations are BOLTED, which is unusual on this cliff and does not carry through to the upper pitches. Count them if in doubt: bolted anchors low, natural gear higher. Negative markers: if you have carried on past the end of the trail and are traversing left along the foot of the cliff, you are walking toward the other documented line and will end up under a low-angle mossy slab rather than a roof; if the first thing above you is easy moss-and-face climbing to a tree belay, you have gone too far left.

bivy.name: Park Creek Camp, at the valley road
bivy.notes: This is the camp the park itself points overnight parties to now that Flat Creek is shut, and that closure is the single most important planning fact for this peak. The camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, which would otherwise be the obvious base, has its access trail closed for hazard trees and has dropped out of both the park's camp list and its booking system; no reopening date has been given anywhere. Park Creek sits lower down the same road, so using it lengthens an approach that is already long — you are walking further to the trailhead each morning rather than sleeping at it. Note this is the camp on the valley road where the Park Creek trail leaves it, not the stock camp several miles up that trail toward the pass. The four-person cap is worth checking against your party before you plan around it.
bivy.water: Park Creek at the camp, reliable all season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, arranged by email before you travel as above. A total campfire ban has been in force across the entire Stehekin valley since the end of June, covering anything that produces ash including propane fire pits, with no end date announced — so the ring here is out of use regardless of what the camp table says about fires. Gas and propane STOVES are still allowed, with clearance around them and a working shut-off valve. Confirm the ban's status when you get the permit.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, each capped at four people, so this is a small-party camp only. No stock. It has a fire ring, which is not the same as permission to use it right now.

bivy.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
bivy.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail of about four miles that gains only a few hundred feet through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. The trail ends well short of the head of the valley and the summit is beyond where it ends. Budget four days minimum for something that would be an afternoon if a road came near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window; the valley walk is snow-free long before the head of it is.
bivy.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
bivy.permit: The agency changes on this trail, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the national forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside that wilderness. It takes a free self-issue permit filled in at the trailhead rather than a park permit, with no reservation and no fee, and a party limit of twelve counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's limit down in the valley, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. Your park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is no park cross-country zone for Flat Creek; that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice otherwise: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury, and no fires.
bivy.capacity: No established camping and no site count. There is nothing up here. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.

bivy.name: Tumwater Camp, Stehekin valley road
bivy.notes: The first camp of consequence above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge, and its job on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day and the last shuttle up the valley goes in the late afternoon, so nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on day one — you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way up the old road, and sleep in flat riverside forest with no view and no alpine character at all. It has a history of high-water damage and was closed after a bad flood, though it stands in the park's current camp table; confirm it is genuinely open when you arrange the permit rather than assuming, because there are not many camps up here and losing one reshapes the whole itinerary.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River is right there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river carrying silt and everything else off the drainage.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park. There is no permit desk in Stehekin — the visitor centre at the landing does not issue them and is closed. For a trip starting in the valley the permit is arranged by EMAIL with the park's wilderness office, sent early on the morning before your start date, with a short mandatory video to watch and a signed copy to print and carry. There is no cell service in Stehekin, so all of that has to happen before you get on the boat. Food lockers are provided at these valley camps and no bear canister is required.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, each taking up to six people, so six is the party ceiling. No stock. Assigned by night on the permit.

bivy.name: Shady Camp, Stehekin valley road
bivy.notes: Further up the old road than Tumwater and the only camp on this stretch that is held back from the booking system entirely, which is exactly why it is worth knowing about. A party whose permit request comes back with a hole in the middle of the itinerary can often fill it here. It is another flat forested river camp with nothing to look at, used purely for position. Note that the road above the washout is closed to BICYCLES as well as vehicles — the upper section is decommissioned or maintained as a non-motorized, non-mechanized trail, so the obvious idea of riding the old roadbed to save a day is not permitted. It is walking or stock, and that is what makes this approach as long as it is.
bivy.water: River water beside the camp, dependable through the season and needing treatment.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, arranged the same way as the rest of the valley — by email to the wilderness office the morning before you start, since nothing can be issued in Stehekin itself. Because the site is walk-up rather than reservable, it cannot be locked in months ahead; ask for it in that same email.
bivy.capacity: A single site taking up to eight people. No stock. Walk-up only — this one takes no reservations at all, which makes it the useful fallback when everything else on the road is booked out.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth near milepost 96.5.

Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot and climb the steep hill to Logger's Ledge. Do not stop there: traverse the ledge east and then keep climbing a long, steep hillside above it. Reckon on roughly 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from Logger's Ledge to the rock.

This crag closes annually. Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock are seasonally closed for peregrine falcon nesting from 1 April until roughly 31 July, or until the young fledge or the Forest Service determines nesting will not occur. That is a repeating yearly pattern, not a one-off notice — plan around it.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — the crag is closed for peregrine nesting for most of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
The route cannot be reached without first leading another pitch to the mid-height ledge
Northwest aspect — cold and shaded in the morning early and late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You reach the left side of Midnight Rock first, coming up and right from Logger's Ledge. Midnight is the tall face — around 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, seamed with parallel-sided cracks — and it faces northwest, so it is in shade through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime is the neighbouring formation and is barely developed; if the wall in front of you has almost nothing on it, you have gone past Midnight.

For ROTC specifically, the crucial fact is that it does not start on the ground. It begins from an enormous ledge that cuts across the middle of the CENTRE part of Midnight Rock, and that ledge is reached by first climbing Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting, or Wasp.

So if you are standing on the deck scanning the wall for a splitter to start up, you are a pitch too low. From the ledge, ROTC is the dead-vertical splitter running from fingers through thin hands to perfect hands, taking gear the whole way to two inches. A line that wanders or changes angle is not it — this crack is straight and plumb.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: Gothic Basin and Weden Pass
approach_variants.notes: Walk the gated Monte Cristo Road from Barlow Pass and take the Weden Creek trail where it splits off on the right just before the road's Sauk River crossing. The trail fords Weden Creek — a real crossing in snowmelt — then switchbacks through forest and talus into Gothic Basin. Leave the maintained tread at the basin and follow a flagged boot path west past two ponds, re-crossing the Weden Creek outlet, then side-hill south across steep talus and heather benches to Weden Pass.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September; the summit register suggests only about one party every four or five years, so expect no track to follow
hazards: The Weden Creek ford runs high during snowmelt and after rain
Exposed, sometimes wet talus traverses between the pass and the summit block — helmet recommended
Loose rock and brush on the class 3-4 summit block, with one short step needing a belay
approach_variants.baseFinding: Weden Pass is where the route-finding starts and the notch north of the main summit block is the thing to find. From the pass, do NOT climb at the first rock you see: the line traverses south-west and LOSES height, dropping to around 4,900 ft along a brushy dirt ramp that skirts underneath the cliff bands, before regaining the notch. The notch is the proof — a distinct gap with a short, steep step above it that is either downclimbed or rappelled, and old webbing is sometimes found on it, which should be treated as years old and replaced with your own rather than trusted. Two wrong answers to guard against. If you traverse west-south-west and arrive at a saddle with two lower rock summits standing to the north of you, that is the saddle between the middle and north peaks and it leads to those, not to the 5,814 ft main summit. And if you are gaining height steadily out of the pass with no descent at all, you have not yet dropped onto the ramp and are above the cliff bands rather than under them.

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
hazards: a steep brushy unmaintained climbers' path with loose rock on the ridge crest
no water between the lake and the moraine tarn
crevasses on both glaciers, with bridges softening through the afternoon
a long crossing with almost no visual reference points, and whiteout navigation as the standing problem
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the west ridge
verglas or rime on the upper rock early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The camp is found by refusing a summit. The climbers' path leads toward Pyramid Peak and the correct move is to drop slightly before it and traverse across scree and boulders to the moraine. If you have scrambled to a summit, you have climbed the wrong peak and gone past the traverse. The arrival marker is a meltwater tarn sitting against a terminal moraine with the ice above it.

From camp the route is a sequence of three pieces of ground and they must come in order. First, rope up before leaving camp and climb the Colonial Glacier south past a rock feature on its east flank, on snow up to about thirty degrees, working around the moraine lake to a broad col near 6,840 ft. A stream runs at that col - a saddle with no water on it is not the right one.

Second, from the col you drop roughly 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped. If you are still gaining height after the col, you have not found the crossing. This is the stretch with no reference points, so track your line for the return; whiteout navigation here is the standing problem of the route.

Third, leave the glacier on the peak's north-west side near a prominent rock feature around 7,700 ft and gain the west ridge by a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing. That puts you three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit. If you are still on ice with the summit pyramid rising straight above you and no gully beside it, you have crossed too far and are under the face rather than the ridge.

The finish is a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, then a short exposed traverse onto the south side and blocky scrambling. You downclimb that notch on the way out, so read it as you pass.

approach_variants.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.
approach_variants.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed saddle camp with weather funnelling through it
a roped carry with overnight loads over crevassed ice
a featureless crossing that is committing in poor visibility from a high camp
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is identified by three things at once: it is broad, it has a stream on it, and the ground beyond it DROPS onto a second, much larger glacier. A saddle that is dry, or one with nothing but rock beyond it, is not this col.

From camp the first move is downhill - 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve - and then a roped crossing on which the cleanest line runs through the centre of the crevasse field. Bridges are usually sound by midsummer and need active route-finding around open slots. Mark your outbound line. Coming back to a col you cannot see, across ground with no features, is the part of this route that goes wrong.

Leave the ice on the peak's north-west side around 7,700 ft, near the prominent rock feature there, and take the class 3 gully with its single exposed rib crossing onto the west ridge, three to four hundred feet below the summit. If there is no gully where you step off the ice, you have gone too far across.

approach_variants.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
approach_variants.season: June through September
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The hardest thing to find on this approach is the path itself, and it is found at a firepit. Walk the closed roadbed uphill through windfall and encroaching brush, crossing two large washouts, until the road ENDS at a small clearing with an old firepit. The climbers' path leaves on the left near that clearing, unsigned and steep from its first step. Fix the spot in your mind on the way in - from above, in fog, it is much harder to find, and parties overshoot it on the descent.

The second decision is a cairned fork near 5,200 ft. A fainter fisherman's trail drops away toward a lake; stay right and uphill on the climbers' path. If you are losing height toward water, you have taken the fisherman's trail.

Expect to lose the tread on the ridge and not to panic about it. Through grass and boulders the path is faint and parties routinely lose it and pick it up again a few hundred feet higher. When in doubt, stay on the crest.

The climb proper starts above the lake meadows. Work round the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A rock wall lines the east side of that outlet; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall itself. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west onto slabs and benches, past small tarns, then traverse rocky slopes to a notch and take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier.

Rope up before stepping onto the snow, not part-way across. If you are trying to climb a rock wall beside the outlet stream, you have missed the turn around its end.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
approach_variants.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever camp you use, the climb starts at the head of the lake's outlet stream. Work counterclockwise round the lake to the outlet. A rock wall runs along the east side of it - the move is to drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of that wall with a single class 3 step. Forcing the wall directly is the wrong answer and is how parties get stopped here.

Above the wall, climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto slabs and benches. Past the small tarns, traverse rocky slopes toward the notch and take the short drop into the gap onto the glacier.

The arrival test is the notch, not the angle. You should step down into a gap to reach the ice. If you have walked onto snow without dropping through a notch, you are on a different bench and should keep traversing.

Cross the glacier to the south-west aiming straight at the peak and leave the snow for rock on the left, where a faint scree path picks up. Sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks finishes it from the south-east ridge or the south slope.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Climb the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, traverse the ledge east, and keep climbing the long steep hillside above — roughly 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge to the rock.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock are closed annually for peregrine falcon nesting, about 1 April to 31 July, or until the young fledge.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
40-45 minutes of sustained steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep coarse granite with scarce moderates
Northwest aspect — cold mornings
approach_variants.baseFinding: You arrive at the left side of Midnight Rock first, coming up and right off Logger's Ledge — that is the fixed point. Midnight is the tall one: around 300 ft of vertical to slightly overhanging coarse granite, mostly parallel-sided cracks, northwest-facing and therefore shaded through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime is the adjacent formation and holds very few routes; a nearly bare wall means you overshot. The crag-wide trap: several of Midnight's best-known lines start from an enormous ledge across the middle of the CENTRE of the wall, not from the ground, and that ledge is gained by leading Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting or Wasp first. Check whether the line you want is a ground start before concluding you cannot find it. No source consulted here documents this route's own position along the base; place it against a topo from the left end.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Three separate routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
The tower in front of the wall carries its own routes under a colliding name
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and then climb scree and talus to the foot of the main wall. Thirty to sixty minutes.

First, rule out the tower. A semi-detached tower leans against the lower right side of the wall, and a deep gully separates it from the mountain. If that tower is between you and the rock, you are under the buttress route, which climbs the ridge behind it. This route is on the open wall, and specifically on its CENTRE. Nothing should be standing in front of you.

Start low and central, near the bottom of the wall rather than off to one side. The line then confirms itself by a run of features in a fixed order, and this is the identification that actually works, because the lower face accepts many lines:

Low down there is a boxed-in feature the first ascent called a confession box. At mid-height there is a spectacular curving chimney — this is the single best confirmation on the route and it is visible from the ground if you look for it. High up you cross a pulpit ledge and then a belfry ledge before easier ground runs to the top.

Negative marker, and it matters because the two lines converge: if instead of a curving chimney you find yourself pushed rightward along a long ramp toward a steep thin crack in a headwall, you have drifted onto the harder line that takes the right-hand third of the face. That one is several number grades above this and it takes very thin protection. Come back left and look for the chimney.
