Second negative marker: the tower in front of the wall has its own small south face carrying several short routes. Beta written about the tower will also be headed South Face. The tower's routes are two to five pitches; this wall is about a thousand feet.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
The wall foreshortens badly from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate at the base
Same walk-off descent with a no-fall gap crossing near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the same and reached the same way from camp. What changes is where you first see the wall, and on a face this size that is worth more than any description.

Coming up the valley you enter the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side stands up in front of you at once. Stop at the lake and sort out three things before walking up: the small detached tower at the lower right of the wall; the deep gully between that tower and the mountain; and the open centre of the wall to the left of both. This route is the open centre.

While you are looking, find the curving chimney at mid-height in that centre panel. It is the feature that proves the line and it is far easier to pick out from across the water than from underneath, where the wall foreshortens and everything reads as featured granite. Fix it against the skyline above it so you can re-find it at the base.

Negative marker from the lake: if the panel you are looking at has a long ramp cutting rightward across it toward a steep headwall crack, that is the right-hand line, not this one. And if the wall you are looking at is only a few pitches tall and stands clear of the mountain, you are looking at the tower.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the standard South Face approach. Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead (about 3,000 ft), PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles to the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction, then #1033 into Commonwealth Basin.

Shortly after the trail crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last water — leave the tread, either right there or after the path has begun to swing up onto Red Mountain's flank, and climb cross-country northwest into the upper basin beneath Lundin's south face.

Expect the same talus and boulder travel, and the same lingering early-season snow in the basin, as the standard route.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail beyond the creek crossing
lingering early-season snow in the upper basin
published route topos disagree on where the line starts
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variation starts near the CENTRE and lowest point of the face, at an obvious layback hand-sized crack. The crack is the identifier, not the position — look for the feature itself.

This matters more here than on most routes: the variation does not start where the original South Face line starts, so a party trying to match an old topo photo will be put in the wrong place. Find the layback crack near the low centre of the face and start there.

If you are on rock with no single obvious crack line, or the crack you have found is off toward one edge of the face rather than near its centre, keep looking along the base rather than committing.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go west along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, with July the usual month; late season the loose ground below the headwall gets worse rather than better
hazards: Frequent rockfall in the cirque and on the headwall, made worse by other parties
Sustained loose scree and choss on the ascent to the cirque, with no trail
A steep eroded descent path off Longs Pass, hard on the knees in both directions
An Ingalls Creek crossing that is a genuine ford in early-season snowmelt
Early-season snow and ice in the cirque
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above the clearing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The cirque is the arrival, and it is unmistakable even in cloud because it closes around you. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

Which clearing, which is the actual problem: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is east of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

Confirmation at the base: the technical pitches start up the CENTRE of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

Preview it from Longs Pass. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor over Itswoot Ridge and Cub Lake and up Bachelor Creek. Off-trail, brushy, and with glacier travel before you reach the peaks; a full day or two of approach is normal. Once in the basin, this route is reached from the lake side rather than from the glacier under the east faces.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the approach is out of snow.
hazards: Long, committing off-trail approach with glacier travel
The cannonhole gap on the traverse pitch is exposed and the feature is relatively young rock
Weather-window dependent — this is a remote crest with no quick way off
Both start dihedrals look alike; picking the wrong one is harmless, picking the wrong face is not
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do not start under the summit — walk south along the foot of the ridge past it. The start is a pair of clean dihedrals side by side on the ridge's west flank, and the pair is the test: two obvious corners, either of which will take you to the crest, with nothing else of the kind nearby. Both give about a rope length of climbing on chickenheads and good face features once you step right out of the corner. The second confirmation is overhead and unmistakable: look along the ridge crest above you for the CANNONHOLE, a gap punched clean through the ridge, which the route traverses on its second pitch. If you cannot see a hole through the crest from where you are standing, you are not below this line. Negative markers: if you are under a single chimney tucked into the left side of a face directly beneath the summit, you have stopped short and are at the west face route; if you are on glacier ice with a moat between you and the rock, you have gone round to the east side entirely.

approach_variants.name: Glacier flank traverse from the east ridge camp
approach_variants.notes: From the parking area on Cascade River Road, backtrack along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River, then take the steep unmaintained climbers' boot path up through old-growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine basin above. Camp on the rocks by the broad flat of the glacier — the standard camp for the ordinary east-ridge line — and traverse from there. Overnight stays need a free backcountry permit.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the glacier flank snow has consolidated but before the ground above the notch melts out to loose scree
hazards: The traverse to the base is steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier — crampons are mandatory
Ground above the ridge is broad and turns to loose scree when melted out
Glacier travel with crevasse-rescue gear is required to reach camp at all
approach_variants.baseFinding: Seen from the glacier on the standard camp approach, this route is the left-hand skyline. The right-hand one is the ordinary way up — a broad snow crest leading to the summit arete — so the first check is simply which of the two skylines you are under. Pick the LOWEST point on the left skyline and traverse the flank of the glacier to it; that traverse is steep, exposed snow and crampons are not optional. The base is then proved by a single feature you can see from the snow before committing: an obvious crack running up the face directly above you to a U-shaped notch cut into the ridge crest. The crack and the U-notch are one thing and either alone is not enough. If there is no U-notch above the crack you have picked, you are too high or too far along the ridge, and the ground there rolls back into loose scree. If you are walking on broad snow with nothing but a snow crest above you, you are on the ordinary route and not on this climb at all.

approach_variants.name: The correct gully off the Quien Sabe, then two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and a rappel to reach the face
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small unsigned Boston Basin pulloff near 3,200-3,300 ft. The old mining road runs about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, then an unmaintained but well-travelled boot path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams — top off bottles there — to treeline around 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on the knoll above the green meadows at 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up and traverse east along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully below the tower. If a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left give an alternate entry and rejoin the couloir about 100 ft up.

There is no separate approach to the Southeast Face. You reach it by climbing the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and rappelling.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, the same window as the Southeast Ridge; being steeper rock it sheds snow a little faster after an early-season storm
hazards: Getting into the wrong gully: on 10 July 2005 a six-person party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here, a climber was struck by rockfall during the roped traverse back toward the standard line, and minutes later a natural boulder anchor failed during the retreat rappel, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth
Loose rock and rockfall in the approach gully, worsening as the season progresses
Crevasse hazard on the upper Quien Sabe Glacier
The two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains and no rap rings, and there is no anchor at all at the very base of pitch 1
Frequent bear activity at Boston Basin camps; food canisters required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This face is not walked to. It is rappelled into — and that is the cleanest test on the whole tower. A party standing at its start has already climbed the first two pitches of the southeast ridge and made two rappels of about 75 ft each from the fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2. A party that WALKED to where it is standing is at the Southeast Ridge notch, one route to the side.

You can see the face from that notch, which is why the mix-up happens: the clean southeast face is visible from the base of the Southeast Ridge and looks approachable. It is not, from there.

Identify the ridge notch by its anchor, not by its shape: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 carries no chains and no rap rings. That absence is a positive identification, and it is also a planning fact — you will be leaving a biner, a ring or a short cord to get down.

Before any of that, get the approach gully right, because this is where people have died. Traverse east along the top of the Quien Sabe several hundred feet; the correct gully leads to a snow patch directly at the tower's base and then a short gully to the notch. A similar-looking gully nearby does not. If your gully does not deliver you to a snow patch at the foot of the tower, stop and re-check rather than continuing or traversing across — the 2005 accident happened during exactly that correction, not during the mistake.

Confirm on the first moves of the face itself: pitch 1 steps onto a detached block and then follows a widening finger-to-ring-lock seam that zig-zags just left of the arete to a bolted anchor in a notch. If you are not standing on a detached block, you are not on this pitch.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col between the two Mox summits is the whole navigation, and the trap is that there are two summits. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

At the col, check which tower you are under. This route is on the eastern summit, which is the harder and higher of the pair. If the peak above you is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, you are facing the western summit and have turned the wrong way out of the saddle.

The sequence above the col is a ladder of specific shapes, in order, and it is how you know you are right: a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief descent to a small flat area. The flat spot after a downclimb is the confirmation - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

From that flat area, locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. If you are uncoiling a rope at the col itself, you are hundreds of feet too low.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
approach_variants.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From either camp the route meets at the same place: the saddle between the two Mox summits, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

The high camp's own marker is that it sits on rock outcrops at the glacier's edge at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

At the saddle, the summit you want is the eastern one - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

The confirmation sequence is the same ladder: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short DOWNCLIMB to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.

bivy.name: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
bivy.notes: This is the working start for Sperry Peak, and Sperry is honestly a day objective with no camp of its own — parties leave from here in the dark, ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, grind up through the talus of Wirtz Basin under Morning Star, take the switchbacked chute to Headlee Pass and traverse under Sperry's south side before scrambling the summit blocks. The only established camp on that line lies beyond the pass in the upper Vesper Creek basin, which the earlier upper-loop file already carries, so the realistic choice here is a long day from the car or a night in that basin. Sleeping at the road end is what most parties do and it works: the spur is short, and a pre-dawn start gets you through the chute before the day's rockfall gets going. Three things decide whether the trip happens at all. The ford half a mile in is the real gate and it is not a formality — it runs hard in snowmelt and log crossings that worked one season are gone the next. The chute below Headlee Pass is loose, narrow and known for rock coming down it, so parties should not stack up in it and helmets belong on well before the base. And snow holds in that chute and on the pass long after the valley is bare, which regularly turns a June or early-July attempt around. The spur itself is rough with potholes and encroaching brush; a low car can usually manage it slowly but scrapes are common. There is no cell coverage from the moment you leave the main loop road.
bivy.water: None at the road end. The creek crossings begin half a mile in and the first of them is the difficult one, so load every litre down in the valley rather than planning to draw here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass to leave a vehicle, and nothing else. This is national forest but NOT designated wilderness, so there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no party-size cap. Overnight parking is allowed. Fires at the road end are governed by whatever seasonal forest-wide restrictions are running, which from midsummer usually means no open flame at all.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only. A small gravel turnaround at the end of the spur with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and no sites, tables or pads. It overflows onto the road shoulder on summer weekends and the last cars in walk a fair way back to the trail start.

bivy.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
bivy.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.
bivy.permit: A developed fee campground on national forest land — the per-night fee is all that is needed and no pass or permit applies to the site itself. Nothing here is inside wilderness. Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, the fixed-rope climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
Drive east over Washington Pass and park in the turnout about two miles beyond it, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. This is a highway pullout, not a trailhead — nothing is signed.

The climbers' path leaves the west or south-west end of the turnout and drops steeply through loose dirt and rock into the trees. It is well worn but unmarked apart from intermittent cairns. It crosses Early Winters Creek on logs and resumes on the far side, then climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation.

Higher up the old line uses two or three fixed lines on an avalanche path before topping out on a flat area. A newer variation bears right just before the fixed lines are reached and needs only a small amount of scrambling; most parties now prefer it. Reckon roughly an hour and a half.

Do not treat the fixed ropes as maintained equipment. They are informal, weathered, and nobody replaces them on a schedule.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and the approach snowfield have melted out
hazards: Weathered informal fixed ropes on the old approach line; the newer right-bearing variation avoids them
Early Winters Creek is crossed on logs and is worse in high water
Long unroped scrambling between pitches on a route people rack up for as a 5.7
Rappelling the line is slow and ropes snag on flakes, sometimes needing re-ascent to free them
The alternative descent gully is loose and sits above the approach path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The marker at the base is dead trees. As the ground steepens toward the formation and before the gully, look on your left for tree snags — standing dead timber against the rock. The first pitch climbs cracks up from a snag. That is the start, and it is the only start on this formation with a landmark you can walk up and touch.

If you have entered the gully itself, you have gone too far right. The gully parallels this route and is used both as a descent and as a fast way to reach the bolted line beside it — it is not this climb.

Confirm on pitch two, which is the strongest check the route gives you: it traverses under a roof. If your second pitch runs sideways beneath an overhang rather than straight up, you are on line. Above that expect steepening ground with cracks and a good layback, then a wide ten-inch crack with finger and hand sections, then a corner crack to lieback, and a headwall finish.

Expect long scrambling sections between the pitches. That is this route's defining character and the main complaint about it — it is the reason a 5.7 with seven pitches takes a full day. Continuous roped climbing with no walking between would mean you are somewhere else.

Negative markers for the two neighbours. If you have traversed a long way rightward from the base on third and fourth-class ledges toward the middle of the face before starting, you are heading for the hard line that finishes on this route's last pitches. And if your first pitch is protected by BOLTS, you are on the partly bolted line — this route takes natural gear throughout.

Descent is most often a rappel of the line itself, and parties report it is slow and that ropes snag on flakes. The alternative is the third-class gully to climbers' right, faster but loose; stay high and skier's-right to limit what is above you.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core Enchantments to the middle of the south face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then climb Aasgard Pass — about 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose scree, the physical crux of the approach. Into early July, snow can bridge a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; that hazard has caused serious injuries and at least one death.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, drop gently into the upper Core basin and travel cross-country north over slabs and heather past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, the usual bivy. The base of the south face is roughly fifteen to twenty minutes from there.

Overnight camping in the Core Zone needs a permit, so many parties do the whole thing in one long day instead.

When Aasgard or this trailhead is closed, the Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative, reaching the same face past Lake Viviane.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is clear of the snow that bridges the creek beneath it
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the last stretch, with no tread
A flaring squeeze chimney at mid-height that is awkward with a pack
A shared north-side rappel descent that gets congested when several parties are on the face
Snafflehounds at the base and at bivy sites will chew boots and gear left out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the route in the middle, and that is the first and most useful fact. Walking along the foot of the south face, the start sits at about the middle of the base. The lines on the left flank of the face all top out on the West Ridge; this one is the classic that goes to the actual summit.

The feature test: you are looking for a chimney system on steep white granite. Pitch one takes either a 5.6/5.7 chimney or a wide crack immediately left of that chimney, and lands on low fifth-class ground with trees on it. Trees at the top of your first pitch is a good confirmation.

How to tell it from its two neighbours, which is the actual problem on this face because three routes start within a hundred feet of each other:
  - If you can see two prominent V-SHAPES on the face and you are at a chimney to the left of them, you are at Beckey-Davis — one route too far right.
  - If you are about fifty feet left of where you think the standard line is, you are at Der Sportsman, and its first pitch is 5.11+ rather than 5.7. A first pitch that feels desperate is the loudest possible signal you are on the wrong route.

Starting coordinate, published for pitch one: roughly 47.48681, -120.78457. In fog with a GPS that is decisive; on a clear day the shape of the face is better.

And the arrival confirmation higher up: pitch five squeezes between a chockstone into a flaring chimney, and pitch six is a left-facing corner to the summit. If your route runs out on the West Ridge instead of the summit, you are on one of the left-flank lines.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, then traverse the ledge east and climb the long steep hillside above — about 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close annually for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep approach hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep, coarse granite; the moderates here are scarce
Northwest aspect — shaded and cold in the morning
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up and right from Logger's Ledge you meet the left side of Midnight Rock first. Midnight is the tall, vertical-to-overhanging face of about 300 ft, full of parallel-sided cracks and facing northwest; Noontime alongside it is barely developed, so a near-empty wall means you have walked too far. This route matters as an access line as much as a climb: Stevens Pass Motel is one of the three routes — with The Sting and Wasp — used to reach the enormous ledge that runs across the middle of the CENTRE section of Midnight Rock. ROTC and other lines start from that ledge rather than the ground. So the confirmation that you are in the right part of the wall is what is above you: a large mid-height ledge system cutting the centre of the face. If there is no such ledge overhead, you are at the wrong end of the crag. No source consulted for this pass gives this route's own start marker at ground level; confirm against a topo.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes:
Oversized dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth — the crag is visible from the road.

For the Lower Wall, walk from the lower, eastern end of the pullout about fifty yards downhill to pick up the climbers' trail, which then climbs steeply to the base. There is also a short trail from the right of the parking area that leads directly to The Fault.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
Highway noise and proximity — the crag is right beside US-2
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first thing to get right is which trail you are on. Two paths leave the same pullout: the one from the uphill, western end traverses east onto Logger's Ledge and serves Upper Castle. If your path is climbing away east onto a big bench, you are heading for the wrong half of the crag.

The Fault is the leftmost of the Lower Wall's selected routes as they run west to east — The Fault, then Catapult, The Vertebrae, The Bone — and it is the route the short trail from the right of the parking area leads to directly.

The Lower Wall as a whole is recognised by its ROOFS: this half of the formation is described as identified by many roofs, and it sits directly beneath Logger's Ledge. So if there is a wide bench above you and roofs overhead, you are in the right half; if you are standing on that bench, you have gone one wall too high.

Two pitches from here reach Logger's Ledge, and a trail leads from the ledge back down to the parking area.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the Cathedral-Monk gully
approach_variants.notes:
Paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft, then twelve miles of trail #504 to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, mostly through an old burn: hot, rocky, buggy and shadeless. Down into the next drainage, then a side trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft.

This is a two-to-four day backpack for almost everyone, climbing from camp in the basin. Free self-issue wilderness permit and a parking pass at the trailhead.

Alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentler and longer, and the high trail from Loomis, shortest on foot but two hours more driving and 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Five unmarked route starts within a few minutes' walk on one small tower
Zigzagging line makes rope drag a real hazard; long slings are essential
Its descent is the tower's rappel gully, not the mountain's walk-off; do not follow summit beta
Descent anchors are not documented as fixed; carry webbing and rings
Remote basin, multi-day walk out, no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The objective is the small semi-detached tower at the lower right of the mountain's south wall, not the wall itself. Walk from camp toward the deep gully between the two and get onto the tower's own rock on the right side of that gully.

This line is the right-hand one on the tower's south face, and it has the only start on this face you can actually stand on and name: a large ledge low down, near the right side of the lowest part of the rock. Walk the base rightward until you can step up onto a ledge big enough to organise a rack on. That is the start. If you are standing on broken talus at the very bottom of the face with no ledge under you, keep walking right.

The route then confirms itself by BEHAVIOUR rather than by a landmark: it ZIGZAGS. Five pitches that keep cutting back and forth across the right side of the face, which is why long slings are not optional here — rope drag is the thing people complain about, and drag is itself evidence you are on the correct line.

Negative markers. If you started at the lowest point of the face and went straight up the middle past a prominent roof, you are on the central line. If your first two pitches were a chimney or gully left of centre, you are on the three-pitch crack line further left. If you started at a pair of parallel cracks on the lower left and were off after two pitches, you are on the short cracks.

Also worth knowing: this route's descent is not the mountain's summit walk-off. It comes off the tower by the north-east gully in three rappels of about seventy-five feet, each covered by a doubled sixty-metre rope. If somebody has told you to walk west off the summit, they were describing the mountain, not the tower.

approach_variants.name: Terror Basin, the upper Barrier crossing and the Degenhardt col
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead the climbers' path parallels the creek on easy old roadbed before a punishing push to treeline in Terror Basin — faint tread, dense brush, and class 3 root-pull sections through cliff bands. Most parties reach the basin in one long day. From the basin cross the Barrier at its upper notch, near 6,200 ft, by way of heather benches and loose rock and moats, into Crescent Creek Basin below the peaks. A direct line into Crescent Creek Basin exists but is buggier and less consistent.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September, once the Crescent and Terror Creek approach is snow-free enough to be reliably passable
hazards: Broken, loose ground working across to the notch
Rock quality flips repeatedly between clean gneiss and dirt-covered choss
A few low fifth-class moves off the ridge crest with no easy retreat
The lower Stump Hollow Barrier crossing leads to a different objective and is the wrong one here
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col between this peak and Degenhardt is the base, and the climbing starts by dropping a few low fifth-class moves off the crest at the col onto the peak's western side — you do not start below the col and climb up to it. The proof once you are on that side is a gully or couloir system leading up and right toward the summit with a band of clearly OVERHANGING rock capping it directly above. The line stays left inside the gully and avoids that overhang entirely; parties who take the roof head-on have found the hard and unnecessary way. Two negative markers. If you crossed the Barrier at the lower Stump Hollow notch rather than the upper one near 6,200 ft, you are set up under a different peak entirely. And a stretch of rubbish, dirt-covered rock is not on its own evidence you are off route here, because this peak's rock alternates between surprisingly solid gneiss and choss on the same face.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, traverse the ledge east and climb the long steep hillside above — 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close annually for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July, or until the young fledge.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
40-45 minutes of steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep, coarse granite
Northwest aspect — cold mornings
approach_variants.baseFinding: You reach the left side of Midnight Rock first off Logger's Ledge. Midnight is the tall face of around 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, seamed with parallel-sided cracks and facing northwest, so it is shaded through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime beside it is nearly undeveloped. The Sting is one of the three lines — with Stevens Pass Motel and Wasp — that get you to the enormous ledge crossing the middle of the CENTRE section of the wall, from which ROTC and others start. So the feature confirming you are in the right sector is that mid-height ledge system directly overhead. No ledge above you means you are at the wrong part of the crag. No source consulted here documents this route's exact position along the base; use a topo from the left end of the wall.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, base gully
approach_variants.notes: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, about 8.5 miles from Leavenworth). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599: the first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest along Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, stay right at the signed junction with the Lake Stuart Trail. The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, two and a half to three hours at a steady pace. Fill water here; it is the last reliable source. Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history. Break off climber's-left through the band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the walk in, 15 to 20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below the main wall.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slick log bridges over Mountaineer Creek in high early-season flow
Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band
Loose 3rd/4th class ground in the final scramble to the wall
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Tempest begins at the CENTRE of the face, below the long bulge and roof, roughly mid-way along the base of the wall — a little right of where the West Face starts out of the gully. The overhanging bulge above is the feature to sight on: if there is no roof over your head, you are either left at the West Face's gully start or right toward The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble; many parties rope up for it. Three and a half to four hours trailhead to base.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout near milepost 166, go directly uphill to the north through talus and forest toward the gully below the wall, taking the forced dogleg out left and back in. Pass the lower ledge and keep going to the upper ledge. There is an exposed easy-fifth step in the gully on the way, so this is not a walk with your hands in your pockets. Rockfall in the gully is worse when another party is above you and worse again after rain.
approach_variants.season: July to September; the highway over the pass is gated shut through winter and into spring, so the wall is car-inaccessible for roughly half the year.
hazards: Loose talus and an exposed easy-fifth step in the approach gully
Rockfall in the gully, particularly with parties above or after rain
South-facing aspect gives full-day sun and real heat in summer
Two routes leave the same treed ledge — confirm which anchor you are heading for before you commit to a rope length
approach_variants.baseFinding: On the upper ledge, work to the CENTRE of the wall — this line is neither the right-hand cave line nor the apron below. The start is a treed ledge, and it is shared: two routes leave from the same spot, so identify it by the ledge and the trees, then identify the route by where you stop. The first pitch here is short — a slabby left-facing corner, about twenty-five metres, ending at a belay well below the first roof. Negative markers: if you run the same corner out to more than sixty metres and finish at a pin-and-gear anchor tucked under a roof, you are on the free variation of the old aid line, which shares this ground; if the corner you started up is forty metres long and leads to a stance under twin left-slanting cracks, you are on the right-hand cave line; and if you are on a narrow ledge below the whole wall with a single bolt beside you, you stopped one ledge too low.

approach_variants.name: Trail #641 to Tin Can Gap, then a glacier-side camp
approach_variants.notes: Identical approach to the other two summits as far as the glacier: the long bike or walk past the permanent road washout to the trailhead, then the trail to the small lake at about two and a half miles, the open meadows at about four and a half, and the GAP at roughly six to seven miles where the maintained tread ends. From the gap drop about four hundred feet off-trail onto the glacier and cross it. Most parties bivy on or near the glacier below the peaks rather than trying all three summits in a push, and this route in particular is normally done from such a camp rather than from the gap.
approach_variants.season: Summer. The moat and any open crevasses drive the timing more than the rock does.
hazards: Loose, suspect rock in the upper part of the scramble, with rockfall onto anyone below
Glacier travel and crevasse risk on the shared approach
A moat between rock and ice that widens through the season
Very little published route detail for this summit — treat it as a lightly documented alpine objective and be prepared to route-find
Fog on the glacier has triggered multiple multi-hour rescues on this mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the glacier-side camp, this summit's south face is reached by a short climb and traverse straight to the foot of the peak — and the discriminator against its northern neighbour is the absence of a col: you do not gain a saddle first and you do not climb a thousand feet on the far side of the glacier before touching rock. If you have gained a col, you are on the wrong tower. The face is BROADER than it looks from the ice, so pick the line from the glacier before you start up; the lower rock is solid third and fourth class and it turns looser and more broken higher, which is the confirmation you are on the described line rather than a cleaner variation. Negative markers: if you are following a ramp leftward into a shallow chimney out of a saddle, you are on the northern tower's route; if you are under three stacked wooden ladders pinned into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the far southern end of the ridge.

rappel_detail.pull: On two 70s this is close to a full-length rappel, so set the knot well clear of the lip and knot the ends.
rappel_detail.notes: Top anchor allowing a rappel from the very top of the route with double 70m ropes.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted station ~20-30 ft above the old P6 slung-block anchor
hazards: Rope choice is decided at this station and the margin is not discretionary: from the top anchor two 70 m ropes reach the bolted anchor atop pitch 5, and doubled 60 m ropes do not reach between them
The older slung-block anchor below the bolts is still the more obvious thing to see; it is not the current station
rappel_detail.station: The top station is a BOLTED anchor sitting roughly 20-30 ft above the old slung-block anchor at the top of pitch 6 - the old block is the landmark, the bolts are above it. Parties on doubled 60 m ropes cannot reach the pitch-5 anchor from here and must stop at the fixed nut-and-sling anchor about halfway down pitch 6.

rappel_detail.notes: Described generically as an 'obvious, good-quality anchor'.
hazards: Slab above and below with little to stand on, so arrive at the anchor rather than near it - there is nothing to grab if you end up off line
rappel_detail.station: The bolted anchor at the top of pitch 5, immediately above the route's very thin slab crux. This is the station the first rappel is measured to, and the reason two 70 m ropes are the published requirement.

rappel_detail.notes: Same as above; individual rappel lengths aren't known.
Continuing down the route on double ropes.
Continuing down the route on double ropes.

rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted or tree anchor near base
hazards: Pitch 1 is described as sustained, heady and delicate with alpine crumbliness - the loosest ground on the route, and both strands run over it
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel, down pitch 1 to the base of the wall.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout to the treed ledge, then its left side and rightward across slabs to the first bolt
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the East Face: from SR-20, park at the informal pullout on the north shoulder of the highway a short walk east of the small pond, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass. No permit needed.

A well-beaten climbers' trail leaves the east end of the pond and climbs steeply through timber; in roughly 30 minutes it breaks out at the edge of the large boulder and talus field that lines the eastern base of the Liberty Bell group, meaning Liberty Bell, Minuteman, Concord and Lexington Towers. From there, work up and left across the talus toward Lexington Tower's east side, 30-45 minutes total from the car for most parties. No reliable water; the roadside pond is not worth using.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
Doubled 60 m ropes do not reach the first rappel station from the top of the route
Surviving original 1989 bolts and an aging fixed-nut anchor despite rebolting
The walk-off traverse borders on unprotected fifth-class slab; many parties stay roped
No water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Tooth and Claw begins near the left side of the treed ledge and angles rightward across slabs to the first bolt. Those are three checkable things in sequence: the left end of a ledge with trees on it, a rightward line across SLABS, and a bolt.

Getting onto the ledge is the first problem and snow decides it: either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow in the talus and at the base into early-mid summer determines whether you gain it from the left or the right. Helmet up well before committing to either gully; both see fairly frequent rockfall.

The discriminator against the route that shares this ledge: the east face, 5.9-plus and ten pitches, is the other line here. This one is 5.12a and it is the one that traverses right off the left end of the ledge to a bolt. If you are starting up cracks from the middle of the ledge without traversing, you are on the East Face.

Hardware as a check, and it is a mixed signal worth reading carefully: the descent stations lower on the route are described as obvious, good-quality anchors on trees or bolts, but some original 1989 quarter-inch-class bolts remain despite a post-2016 rebolting push, and at least one older fixed-nut and sling anchor is noted as aging. New-looking bolts are not proof of a modern line here.

Descent, and the rope length is the binding constraint: from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 ft above the old pitch-6 slung-block anchor. With double 70 M ropes you can rappel from the very top; doubled 60 M ropes will not reach that first station. Most parties instead take the walk-off from the East Shoulder: an exposed, somewhat sketchy fourth-class traverse west, bordering on unprotected fifth-class slab in spots, to gain the same descent gully the East Face uses.

wa_unnamed_5.rope_note: Spire Gully right - Alpenkuhl. Recorded as 5.8+, TRAD (only trad route in this otherwise-bolted cluster) - needs a real rack, not just draws.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek, Itswoot Ridge and the Dome-Chikamin col
approach_variants.notes: This is a two-day approach each way and there is no short way in. From the Downey Creek Trailhead follow the valley trail to the Bachelor Creek crossing, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path through heavy brush to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge for the first camp. From there continue over the ridge and glacier ground to the Dome-Chikamin col and make a high camp. On the climbing day, cross the Chikamin Glacier from the col to the foot of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn; the glacier crossing opens up as the season goes on and later parties have reached the ice by the rock rib coming down off the neighbouring summit instead
hazards: Big crevasses on the Chikamin Glacier; the bergschrund is crossed on a snow bridge and is a place to move quickly
Heavy bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
Sustained hard free climbing on a very steep face, two days from the car in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cross the glacier from the col to the foot of the face and then stop looking at the wall — the start is not reached from the ice. Get onto the ramp that runs beneath the left side of the face and scramble along it. The ramp SPLITS, and the route starts just past that split, with a small cairn on the ground marking it. Those two things together, the split in the ramp and the cairn beside it, are the proof; either on its own is not enough on a face this size. From there the first climbing goes up a shallow corner on thin cracks, flakes and occasional knobs on clean white granite, and the objective is the centre of the wall. If you are still on the glacier below a uniformly steep face with no ramp beneath you, you have not gained the access ledge. If the ramp is running on unbroken with no branch in it, keep going — you are short of the start.

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib to the bench, then the contour right
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain above rather than for the spires, and nothing marks the climbers' path.

The path drops down the talus and into the forest, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log, and then climbs steeply up the timbered rib on the left — the north side — of the creek that drains the col above. Two hours or so of steep walking puts you on the basin bench at about 6,500 ft. There is a spring near the bench camp and it is the last reliable water.

From the bench the trail continues another three-quarters of an hour to the col at about 7,720 ft, which is the hub for the whole cluster. This route does not need to go that far.

The pullout doubles as the overnight for most parties. Nothing there is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access disappears when the highway closes
hazards: Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path with no trail signs anywhere
The start is a single jammed block; the lower ridge offers several plausible wrong starts
The final pitch is runout exposed face climbing with marginal protection
Rope drag on the long crest pitch if slings are not managed
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route starts lower than everything else in the cluster, and that is the fact to hold onto. The spires above the col get climbed from the col; this one does not.

Leave the col trail at the bench, around 6,600 ft, and contour right — south — around the bench toward the pinnacle's lower section. You are aiming for the toe of the ridge rather than for anything above you. There is a dry sandy gully on this contour with a spring in it, which is a useful confirmation that you are on the right ground and the last water before the climb.

The start itself is marked by a CHOCKSTONE — a jammed block at the foot of the ridge. That chockstone is the identification, and it is the reason accounts of this route keep saying to pay attention to the topo: without it, the lower ridge offers several plausible ways on and parties have burned an hour sorting it out.

If you come at it from the col instead, drop about two hundred feet of mostly fourth-class rock to sandy ledges just left of the pinnacle's top and work down and along; that reaches the same ground from above.

Confirm on the climb. Seven or eight pitches of sustained mid-fifth-class hand and finger cracks along the ridge crest, with big comfortable belay ledges. The technical crux is about halfway up, on the fourth pitch, on a short section of steep twin finger cracks. The last pitch is exposed, runout face climbing that most parties call the real crux for reasons that have nothing to do with the grade.

Negative marker: if you walked all the way to the col, then dropped a few hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank onto a third-class ledge system and walked it rightward to a steep clean corner, you are at the other route on this pinnacle, several number grades harder. A ledge system leading to a corner is not this climb; a chockstone at the toe of a ridge is.

Second negative marker: the neighbouring spire's north face is the usual link-up partner and its routes start from the col itself. Being at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are at this route.

Descent is a few hundred feet of downclimbing, then two rappels of about thirty and twenty metres into the gully beneath the col, downclimbing between the anchors, then the trail back past the bench.

approach_variants.name: Monte Cristo and Glacier Basin
approach_variants.notes: From Barlow Pass walk the gated road to the old townsite; the road is bike-friendly and the river crossing near the first mile is a large log or a ford, with no bridge. Surface water near the townsite can carry arsenic and metals from old tailings, so treat or carry it. Past the townsite the Glacier Basin trail turns very steep and climbs wet, slick bedrock beside the falls — poor footing, worst on the descent — to the campsites on the timbered knoll where the maintained trail effectively ends. Leave the trail there and climb steep, very loose talus, or snow early in the season, to the col on the dividing ridge.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the basin talus is snow-free
hazards: Slick wet bedrock beside the falls, especially descending
Steep, very loose talus gaining the col
A short exposed class 3-4 step on the summit block that is not a walk-up
Contaminated surface water near the old townsite
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identification that matters happens at the col on the dividing ridge, because parties from this trailhead routinely commit to the wrong summit. The SPIRES lie along the crest and are slender, detached towers; their routes are all fifth class and roped, and the nearest of them has a famously tiny summit reached by a separate climb. The peak this route goes to is the broad, bulky mass carrying the tall north face, and the line gains it by the north-west ridge from the col. Stand at the col and settle which of the two you are beneath before starting up — a tower with a pointed, detached profile is the wrong answer. The second check is at the top: the final summit block is a short, exposed class 3-4 step on volcanic breccia, so if you have arrived at what you think is the top on pure walking ground with no scrambling move at all, you are on a shoulder and not on the summit.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot up to Logger's Ledge, then traverse the ledge east and keep climbing the long steep hillside above — about 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close every year for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July, or until the young fledge or the Forest Service determines no nesting will occur.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep, coarse granite with few moderate lines
Northwest aspect — shaded and cold in the morning
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up and to the right from Logger's Ledge you arrive at the left side of Midnight Rock first — so the left end of the wall is the fixed point to work from, not the centre. Midnight is the taller of the pair: roughly 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging coarse granite, mostly parallel-sided crack lines, facing northwest so it holds shade through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime sits alongside and is barely developed; if you have walked to a wall with only a handful of routes on it, you have gone past Midnight. Note the general trap at this crag: several of the best-known lines here, ROTC among them, begin from an enormous ledge halfway up the CENTRE of the wall rather than from the ground, and that ledge is reached by climbing another route first. Before assuming a line is unreachable, check whether it is a ground-up start at all. No source consulted for this pass records where Yellow Bird itself starts along the base; identify it against a topo from the left end of the wall.
